glossary.false information intended to misuse a p: Section 217 BNS: giving a public servant information known or believed false, intending or knowing it likely to cause that public servant to act wrongly or to misuse their lawful power to someone's injury or annoyance, punishable with up to one year's imprisonment, fine up to ten thousand rupees, or both.
glossary.false information causing wrongful dismi: The illustrative scenarios under Section 217 BNS: a false neglect-of-duty complaint engineered to get a subordinate officer dismissed, and a false contraband tip engineered to trigger an annoying search of someone's premises -- both captured as examples of misusing a public servant's lawful power through deliberate falsehood.
glossary.resistance to lawful taking of property: Section 218 BNS: offering resistance to the taking of property under the lawful authority of a public servant, knowing or having reason to believe the taker is such a public servant, punishable with up to six months' imprisonment, fine up to ten thousand rupees, or both.
glossary.obstructing a sale of property conducted: Section 219 BNS: intentionally obstructing a sale of property offered for sale under a public servant's lawful authority, punishable with up to one month's imprisonment, fine up to five thousand rupees, or both -- a lighter offence than Section 218's resistance-to-taking.
glossary.illegal purchase or bid at a lawful publ: Section 220 BNS: purchasing or bidding at a public-servant-authority sale on account of a person known to be legally incapable of purchasing at that sale, punishable with up to one month's imprisonment, fine up to two hundred rupees, or both.
glossary.sham bidding without intent to perform: The second limb of Section 220 BNS: bidding for property at a lawful public-servant sale without any genuine intention of performing the obligations the bid creates, punished identically to bidding on behalf of a legally incapable purchaser.
glossary.obstructing a public servant in discharg: Section 221 BNS: the general-purpose obstruction offence -- voluntarily obstructing a public servant while they discharge their public functions, punishable with up to three months' imprisonment, fine up to two thousand five hundred rupees, or both.
glossary.omission to assist a public servant when: Section 222 BNS: intentionally omitting to render assistance to a public servant in execution of public duty, where legally bound to furnish it, punishable with up to one month (escalated to six months where the assistance was demanded for Court-process execution, offence prevention, riot/affray suppression, or apprehending an offender or escapee).
glossary.refusal of posse comitatus-style assista: A description of Section 222 BNS's underlying rationale: the modern statutory equivalent of the common-law duty of ordinary citizens to assist public authority when lawfully called upon, with refusal in serious circumstances (riot suppression, apprehending escapees) drawing the heavier six-month punishment band.
glossary.disobedience to a lawfully promulgated p: Section 223 BNS: knowing disobedience of a lawfully promulgated public-servant order directing abstention from an act or specified property handling, punishable with up to six months where the disobedience causes or risks obstruction/annoyance/injury to a lawfully employed person, escalating to up to one year where it causes or risks danger to life, health, safety, or a riot/affray.
glossary.no-intent-to-harm requirement for order: The Explanation to Section 223 BNS: liability does not require intent to produce harm or contemplation that disobedience is likely to produce harm -- mere knowledge of the order plus disobedience that produces or is likely to produce harm suffices, a comparatively strict liability standard within the Sanhita.
glossary.threat of injury to a public servant to: Section 224 BNS: holding out a threat of injury to a public servant, or to a person believed to interest that public servant, for the purpose of inducing them to act, forbear, or delay in their public functions, punishable with up to two years' imprisonment, fine, or both.
glossary.threat to deter a legal application for: Section 225 BNS: holding out a threat of injury to a person to induce them to refrain from, or abandon, a legal application for protection to a public servant empowered to give it, punishable with up to one year's imprisonment, fine, or both -- an access-to-justice protection complementing Section 224.
glossary.attempt to commit suicide to compel or r: Section 226 BNS, closing Chapter XIII: attempting suicide with intent to compel or restrain a public servant from discharging official duty, punishable with up to one year's simple imprisonment, fine, or both, or with community service.
glossary.giving false evidence: Defined in Section 227 BNS, opening Chapter XIV: making a statement known or believed false, or not believed true, while legally bound by oath, express legal provision, or a legal duty to declare, to state the truth -- the definitional foundation for the punishment provisions in Sections 229-231.
glossary.false statement as to belief: Explanation 2 to Section 227 BNS: a person may give false evidence by falsely stating what they believe, not just what they claim to know -- stating one believes something one does not actually believe is treated the same as falsely claiming knowledge.
glossary.good-faith belief as a defence to false: Illustration (c) to Section 227 BNS: a statement of genuine, good-faith belief is not false evidence even if objectively mistaken -- e.g. believing a signature to be someone's handwriting in good faith, even if it later turns out not to be, is not false evidence because the offence targets dishonesty of mind, not factual error.
glossary.fabricating false evidence: Defined in Section 228 BNS: causing a circumstance to exist, making a false entry in a book/record/electronic record, or creating a document/electronic record containing a false statement, intending it to appear as evidence in a judicial proceeding, public-servant proceeding, or arbitration, and to mislead the fact-finder on a material point -- illustrated by planting jewels to frame someone for theft or forging a letter in someone else's handwriting.
glossary.planting evidence to mislead a fact-find: A description of the core conduct criminalised by Section 228 BNS's fabrication offence -- physically or documentarily manufacturing false circumstances intended to cause a judicial or quasi-judicial fact-finder to form an erroneous opinion on a material point.
glossary.punishment for false evidence in a judic: Section 229(1) BNS: intentionally giving false evidence, or fabricating false evidence for use, in any stage of a judicial proceeding, punishable with up to seven years' imprisonment plus fine up to ten thousand rupees -- the heavier of the two Section 229 bands.
glossary.punishment for false evidence outside ju: Section 229(2) BNS: the lighter residual band for intentionally giving or fabricating false evidence in any case other than a judicial proceeding (e.g. before a non-judicial public servant or an arbitrator), punishable with up to three years' imprisonment plus fine up to five thousand rupees.
glossary.stage of a judicial proceeding: Defined broadly across the three Explanations to Section 229 BNS to include courts-martial trials and both Court-directed and law-mandated preliminary investigations (e.g. a Magistrate's committal enquiry or a Court-deputed boundary investigation) -- even proceedings that never literally occur inside a courtroom can count as a 'stage of a judicial proceeding' for the heavier Section 229(1) punishment.
glossary.false evidence intended to procure a cap: Section 230 BNS: giving or fabricating false evidence intending, or knowing it likely, to cause someone's conviction for a capital offence, punishable with life imprisonment or up to ten years' rigorous imprisonment plus fine up to fifty thousand rupees -- escalating to the death penalty itself if an innocent person is actually convicted and executed as a result.
glossary.enhanced punishment where an innocent pe: Section 230(2) BNS: if an innocent person is actually convicted and executed in consequence of false evidence given under Section 230(1), the false-evidence-giver is liable to the death penalty itself (or the Section 230(1) punishment) -- the outcome, not merely the intent, triggers this maximal tier.
glossary.false evidence intended to procure convi: Section 231 BNS: giving or fabricating false evidence intending, or knowing it likely, to cause someone's conviction for a non-capital offence punishable with life imprisonment or seven-plus years, where the false-evidence-giver's own punishment mirrors exactly what the falsely targeted offence carries.
glossary.mirror-punishment for false evidence tar: The structural principle underlying Section 231 BNS: the punishment for giving or fabricating false evidence to procure a conviction is pegged to the severity of the specific offence being falsely targeted, illustrated by a false witness facing the same life-imprisonment-or-up-to-ten-years exposure as the dacoity charge he tried to engineer.
glossary.threatening a person to give false evide: Section 232 BNS: threatening injury to a person, or to someone in whom they are interested, with intent to induce them to give false evidence, punishable with up to seven years' imprisonment, fine, or both.
glossary.enhanced liability for a threatener wher: Section 232(2) BNS: where an innocent person is actually convicted and sentenced (to death or more than seven years) in consequence of false evidence coerced under Section 232(1), the threatener bears the same punishment and sentence actually imposed on that innocent person.
glossary.using evidence known to be false or fabr: Section 233 BNS: corruptly using, or attempting to use, evidence as true or genuine while knowing it is false or fabricated, punished identically to the person who originally gave or fabricated that evidence under Section 229's bands.
glossary.issuing or signing a false certificate: Section 234 BNS: issuing or signing a legally required certificate, relating to a fact for which it is by law admissible in evidence, knowing or believing it false in a material point -- punished the same as giving false evidence under Section 229.
glossary.using as true a certificate known to be: Section 235 BNS: corruptly using, or attempting to use, a Section-234-type certificate as true while knowing it false in a material point -- the using-side companion to Section 234's issuing/signing offence, punished identically to giving false evidence.
glossary.false statement in a legally receivable: Section 236 BNS: making a statement known or believed false, or not believed true, in a declaration a Court or public servant is bound or authorised by law to receive as evidence of a fact, touching a point material to the declaration's purpose -- punished the same as giving false evidence.
glossary.using as true a declaration known to be: Section 237 BNS: corruptly using, or attempting to use, a Section-236-type declaration as true while knowing it false in a material point -- the using-side companion to Section 236, punished identically to giving false evidence.
glossary.informality does not exclude a declarati: The Explanation to Section 237 BNS: a declaration otherwise inadmissible merely for some technical informality still counts as a 'declaration' for the purposes of both Sections 236 and 237, preventing evasion of liability through a minor procedural defect in the declaration's form.
glossary.causing disappearance of evidence of an: Section 238 BNS: causing evidence of a known or believed-committed offence to disappear, with intent to screen the offender from legal punishment, punishable in three tiers graduated by the underlying offence's severity -- illustrated by someone who helps hide a murder victim's body.
glossary.giving false information to screen an of: The alternative limb of Section 238 BNS: giving false information about a known or believed-committed offence, with intent to screen the offender, carrying the same three-tier graduated punishment as causing evidence of the offence to disappear.
glossary.graduated punishment keyed to the underl: The recurring sentencing structure in Sections 238, 249, 250, 251, and 253 BNS: punishment for obstruction-of-justice conduct (screening an offender, harbouring, taking gifts to screen) is set in tiers according to how serious the underlying offence being screened is -- death-punishable, life-or-ten-years-punishable, or lesser.
glossary.intentional omission to give information: Section 239 BNS: a person legally bound to give information of an offence's commission who intentionally omits to do so, punished with imprisonment and fine scaled to the underlying offence's severity -- the companion omission-offence to Section 211's broader public-servant-information duty, specifically targeted at offence-reporting.
glossary.giving false information respecting an o: Section 240 BNS: giving information respecting an offence's commission that is known or believed false, punishable with up to two years' imprisonment, fine, or both -- the active-falsehood sibling of Section 239's omission offence, both feeding into the Section 238 scheme of screening offenders from justice.
glossary.extraterritorial offence definition for: The shared Explanation across Sections 238, 239 and 240 BNS: 'offence' for the purposes of causing evidence to disappear, omitting to report, or falsely reporting, is extended to specified acts committed outside India that would be offences under the enumerated BNS provisions if committed in India -- preventing offenders who act abroad from escaping the screening-related offences merely because the underlying act occurred outside Indian territory.
glossary.destruction or concealment of a document: Section 241 BNS: secreting or destroying a document or electronic record, or obliterating/rendering it illegible, which one may be lawfully compelled to produce as evidence, intending to prevent its production or to cause a false copy to be given in evidence, punishable with up to three years' imprisonment, fine, or both.
glossary.obliterating or rendering a document ill: The alternative limb of Section 241 BNS alongside secreting or destroying -- obliterating or rendering a document or electronic record illegible with the same intent to prevent its lawful production as evidence, punished identically to outright destruction or concealment.
glossary.false personation in a suit or criminal: Section 242 BNS: falsely personating another person, and in that assumed character, making any admission or statement, confessing judgment, causing any process to be issued, or doing any other act in a suit or criminal prosecution, either with or without that other person's consent -- punishable with up to three years' imprisonment, fine, or both, regardless of whether the impersonated person consented.
glossary.fraudulent removal or concealment of pro: Section 243 BNS: fraudulently removing, concealing, transferring, or delivering possession of any property, intending to prevent that property from being taken as forfeited to the Government or in execution of a decree/order, punishable with up to two years' imprisonment, fine, or both.
glossary.fraudulent claim to property to defeat f: Section 244 BNS: fraudulently accepting, receiving, or claiming property, or any interest in it, knowing that no such right exists, with the same intent to defeat its forfeiture to Government or seizure in execution -- the claiming-side companion to Section 243's removal/concealment offence, punished identically.
glossary.fraudulently suffering a decree or order: Section 245 BNS: fraudulently causing or suffering a decree or order to be passed against oneself for a sum not due, or for a larger sum than is due, or for property/interest in property one does not legally possess, intending to cause that decree/order to be executed against one's own or another's property -- punishable with up to two years' imprisonment, fine, or both, illustrated by a debtor who lets a friend obtain a collusive decree to shield assets from a genuine creditor.
glossary.fraudulently suffering execution of an a: A further limb of Section 245 BNS: fraudulently suffering a decree or order to be executed against oneself after it has already been satisfied, or for anything beyond what is justly due under it -- treated identically to fraudulently suffering the original collusive decree.
glossary.dishonestly making a false claim in Cour: Section 246 BNS: dishonestly making, in a Court proceeding or before a public servant/arbitrator authorised to take evidence, a claim one knows to be false -- punishable with up to two years' imprisonment, fine, or both.
glossary.fraudulently obtaining a decree for a su: Section 247 BNS: fraudulently obtaining a decree or order against another for a sum not due, or for a larger sum than is due, or for property/interest not legally possessed, intending to cause it to be executed -- the obtaining-side mirror of Section 245's suffering offence, same punishment band.
glossary.fraudulently executing an already-satisf: A further limb of Section 247 BNS: fraudulently causing a decree or order to be executed after it has already been satisfied or for anything beyond what is justly due -- the obtaining-side mirror of Section 245's parallel limb, punished identically.
glossary.false criminal charge made with intent t: Section 248 BNS: instituting or causing to be instituted a criminal proceeding against a person, or falsely charging a person with having committed an offence, knowing there is no just or lawful ground for the charge, intending to injure that person -- punishable with up to five years' imprisonment, fine up to two lakh rupees, or both, as the base band.
glossary.aggravated false charge of a serious off: Section 248's escalated tier: where the falsely levelled charge is of an offence punishable with death, life imprisonment, or imprisonment of seven years or more, the punishment for the false charge rises to up to seven years' imprisonment plus mandatory fine -- the charge's own gravity drives the enhancement, mirroring the mirror-punishment logic seen in Section 231's false-evidence provision.
glossary.harbouring or concealing an offender: Section 249 BNS: harbouring or concealing a person known or believed to have committed an offence, or to be liable to apprehension for one, with intent to screen that person from legal punishment -- punished in three tiers graduated by the underlying offence's severity (death-punishable, life/10-years-punishable, or lesser).
glossary.spousal exception to harbouring an offen: The Exception to Section 249 BNS (also mirrored in Section 253): the harbouring offence does not extend to cases where the harbouring is done by the spouse of the offender -- a limited familial carve-out from an otherwise broadly drawn obstruction-of-justice offence.
glossary.taking a gift to screen an offender from: Section 250 BNS: taking a gift, or agreeing to take a gift or restoration of property, as consideration for screening a known or believed offender from legal punishment, or for not proceeding against them -- punished in the same three graduated tiers as Section 249's harbouring offence.
glossary.offering a gift to procure screening of: Section 251 BNS: the offering-side mirror of Section 250 -- providing or offering a gift, or restoration of property, as consideration for an offender's screening from punishment, punished in the same three graduated tiers, subject to the same compoundable-offence exception.
glossary.compoundable-offence exception to Sectio: The shared Exception to Sections 250 and 251 BNS: neither the taking nor the offering of a screening-related gift is an offence where the underlying matter concerns a legally compoundable offence -- aligning the Sanhita's obstruction-of-justice provisions with the ordinary criminal-procedure compounding regime rather than criminalising lawful private settlement of compoundable matters.
glossary.taking a gift to help recover stolen pro: Section 252 BNS: taking a gift under pretence or on account of helping any person recover movable property of which they have been deprived by an offence, without causing the apprehension/conviction of, or giving such information as would facilitate the apprehension/conviction of, the offender -- punishable with up to two years' imprisonment, fine, or both.
glossary.harbouring an escaped-from-custody or ap: Section 253 BNS: harbouring or concealing a person known or believed to have escaped from lawful custody, or for whose apprehension an order has been issued, with intent to prevent their apprehension -- punished in the same three graduated tiers as Section 249, with its own extradition-linked extraterritorial Explanation and the same spousal exception.
glossary.extradition-linked extraterritorial offe: The Explanation to Section 253 BNS: extends the harbouring offence to cover persons who have escaped from custody or are liable to apprehension in respect of acts committed outside India that would constitute offences under Indian law and that are extraditable under applicable extradition law -- tying the domestic harbouring offence to India's extradition framework for offenders fleeing foreign jurisdiction.
glossary.harbouring robbers or dacoits: Section 254 BNS: harbouring persons known or believed to be about to commit, or to have recently committed, robbery or dacoity, with intent to facilitate or screen them, punishable with rigorous imprisonment up to seven years plus fine -- a heavier, offence-specific version of Section 249's general offender-harbouring provision, reflecting the Sanhita's particular concern with organised and violent property crime.
glossary.facilitating or screening robbery or dac: The dual-intent requirement of Section 254 BNS: the harbour must be given either to facilitate the commission of the robbery or dacoity, or to screen the persons involved from punishment -- either intent suffices, and the Explanation makes it immaterial whether the robbery/dacoity is intended within or without India.
glossary.public servant disobeying legal directio: The first limb of Section 255 BNS: a public servant who knowingly disobeys a legal direction governing their own official conduct, intending or knowing it likely that doing so will save a person from legal punishment or reduce the punishment to which they are liable, punishable with up to two years' imprisonment, fine, or both.

The alternative limb of Section 255 BNS: the same knowing disobedience of an official-conduct direction, but aimed instead at saving property from forfeiture or a legal charge -- either limb independently completes the offence, punished identically.
glossary.public servant knowingly framing an inco: Section 256 BNS: a public servant charged with preparing a record or writing who knowingly frames it incorrectly, intending (or knowing it likely) to cause loss or injury to the public or a person, or to save a person from punishment, or to save property from forfeiture -- punishable with up to three years' imprisonment, fine, or both, one year heavier than Section 255's conduct-disobedience offence.
glossary.public servant corruptly making a report: Section 257 BNS: a public servant who corruptly or maliciously makes or pronounces, in any stage of a judicial proceeding, a report, order, verdict, or decision known to be contrary to law, punishable with up to seven years' imprisonment, fine, or both -- targeting deliberate judicial or quasi-judicial corruption, not honest legal error.
glossary.corruptly committing or confining a pers: Section 258 BNS: a person holding legal authority to commit persons for trial or to confinement, or to keep persons in confinement, who corruptly or maliciously exercises that authority knowing it is contrary to law, punishable with up to seven years' imprisonment, fine, or both -- the custody-side companion to Section 257's judgment-side corruption offence.
glossary.intentional omission to apprehend by pub: Section 259 BNS: a public servant legally bound to apprehend or confine a person charged with, or liable to be apprehended for, an offence, who intentionally omits to apprehend them, punishable in three tiers (up to 7 years, 3 years, or 2 years) graduated by the severity of the offence the person was charged with or liable for.
glossary.intentionally suffering or aiding escape: The alternative limbs of Section 259 BNS alongside outright omission to apprehend -- intentionally suffering such a person to escape, or intentionally aiding their escape or attempted escape from confinement, punished identically across the same three severity-graded tiers.
glossary.intentional omission to apprehend a pers: Section 260 BNS: the heavier sibling of Section 259, covering a public servant's intentional omission to apprehend, or suffering/aiding the escape of, a person already under a Court's sentence or lawfully committed to custody (rather than merely charged) -- punishment tiers roughly double those of Section 259, up to life imprisonment or fourteen years where the escapee was under sentence of death.
glossary.negligently suffering an escape from con: Section 261 BNS: the negligence-based residual offence alongside Sections 259-260's intentional omission offences -- a public servant bound to keep a person in confinement who merely negligently (not intentionally) suffers their escape, punishable with up to two years' simple imprisonment, fine, or both, regardless of the escapee's status or underlying offence severity.
glossary.resisting or obstructing one's own lawfu: Section 262 BNS: the flip side of Sections 259-261 -- a person who intentionally offers resistance or illegal obstruction to their own lawful apprehension for a charged or convicted offence, punishable with up to two years' imprisonment, fine, or both, explicitly in addition to punishment for the underlying offence.
glossary.escaping or attempting escape from lawfu: The second limb of Section 262 BNS alongside resistance/obstruction -- escaping, or attempting to escape, from custody in which one is lawfully detained for a charged or convicted offence, punished identically and equally stacked atop the underlying offence's punishment per the section's Explanation.
glossary.resisting or obstructing the lawful appr: Section 263 BNS: the third-party mirror of Section 262 -- intentionally resisting or illegally obstructing another person's lawful apprehension, punished across five escalating tiers (base up to two years, rising to life imprisonment or ten years) keyed to the severity of the offence the apprehended person faces or the sentence they are already serving.
glossary.rescuing or attempting to rescue another: The alternative limb of Section 263 BNS alongside resistance/obstruction -- rescuing or attempting to rescue another person from lawful custody, punished under the same five-tier severity ladder as resisting that person's apprehension in the first place.
glossary.residual omission to apprehend or suffer: Section 264 BNS: the catch-all provision for a public servant's omission to apprehend, or sufferance of escape, in cases not already covered by Sections 259, 260, or 261 -- split into an intentional band (up to three years) and a negligent band (up to two years' simple imprisonment), mirroring those sections' intentional/negligent split.
glossary.residual resistance obstruction escape o: Section 265 BNS: the catch-all counterpart to Section 264, covering resistance, illegal obstruction, escape, or rescue not already covered by Sections 262 or 263, punishable with a single flat band of up to six months' imprisonment, fine, or both -- deliberately lighter than the specifically enumerated scenarios in 262-263.
glossary.knowing violation of a condition of remi: Section 266 BNS: a person who has accepted conditional remission of punishment and knowingly violates a condition of that remission is restored to liability for the original sentence (or whatever unserved portion remains) -- a restorative rather than additive consequence, closing out the public-servant-complicity cluster of Chapter XIV before its final three offences.
glossary.intentional insult or interruption to a: Section 267 BNS: the Sanhita's contempt-of-court-adjacent offence -- intentionally insulting or interrupting a public servant while sitting in any stage of a judicial proceeding, punishable with up to six months' simple imprisonment, fine up to five thousand rupees, or both.
glossary.personation of an assessor: Section 268 BNS: by personation or otherwise, intentionally causing or suffering oneself to be returned, empanelled, or sworn as an assessor while knowing one is not legally entitled to be, punishable with up to two years' imprisonment, fine, or both.
glossary.knowingly serving as an assessor when no: The alternative limb of Section 268 BNS alongside personation -- knowing oneself to have been returned, empanelled, or sworn as an assessor contrary to law, and voluntarily serving on the case regardless, punished identically to engineering one's own unlawful selection in the first place.
glossary.failure to appear in court per bail bond: Section 269 BNS, closing Chapter XIV: a person released on bail bond or bond who fails, without sufficient cause, to appear in Court per the bond's terms, punishable with up to one year's imprisonment, fine, or both -- explicitly stacked on top of punishment for the underlying charged offence and independent of the Court's own bond-forfeiture power under BNSS Section 491.
glossary.burden of proof on the accused to show s: The reversed-burden feature of Section 269 BNS: once the bare fact of non-appearance under a bail bond or bond is shown, the accused bears the burden of proving sufficient cause for it -- unlike most BNS offences, where the prosecution carries the burden throughout.
glossary.public nuisance: Section 270 BNS, opening Chapter XV: an act or illegal omission causing common injury, danger, or annoyance to the public or to people dwelling/occupying property in the vicinity, or necessarily obstructing or endangering anyone exercising a public right -- not excused merely because it also causes some convenience or advantage; Section 292 supplies the residual punishment where no more specific chapter provision applies.
glossary.common injury danger or annoyance to the: The core harm threshold in Section 270 BNS's public-nuisance definition -- injury, danger, or annoyance that affects the public generally or people dwelling/occupying property nearby, distinguishing public nuisance from a purely private wrong affecting only one or a few individuals.
glossary.negligent act likely to spread infection: Section 271 BNS: unlawfully or negligently doing an act one knows or has reason to believe is likely to spread the infection of a disease dangerous to life, punishable with up to six months' imprisonment, fine, or both -- the lighter, negligence-based counterpart to Section 272's malignant-intent version of the same conduct.
glossary.malignant act likely to spread infection: Section 272 BNS: malignantly doing an act one knows or has reason to believe is likely to spread the infection of a disease dangerous to life, punishable with up to two years' imprisonment, fine, or both -- the aggravated-intent counterpart to Section 271, with a maximum sentence four times higher.
glossary.knowing disobedience to a quarantine rul: Section 273 BNS: knowingly disobeying a Government-made rule for quarantining a mode of transport, regulating intercourse of quarantined transport, or regulating movement between infectious-disease-affected places and other places -- punishable with up to six months' imprisonment, fine, or both; a regulatory-compliance offence complementing Sections 271-272's substantive disease-spreading offences.
glossary.adulterating food or drink to make it no: Section 274 BNS: adulterating a food or drink article so as to make it noxious, while intending or knowing it likely that it will be sold as food or drink, punishable with up to six months' imprisonment plus fine up to five thousand rupees -- the manufacturing-side offence paired with Section 275's selling-side mirror.
glossary.selling food or drink known to be noxiou: Section 275 BNS: selling, offering, or exposing for sale as food or drink an article rendered noxious or unfit, while knowing or having reason to believe it is noxious, punished identically to Section 274's adulteration offence -- the seller need not have done the adulterating themselves.
glossary.adulterating a drug or medical preparati: Section 276 BNS: adulterating a drug or medical preparation so as to lessen its efficacy, change its operation, or make it noxious, intending or knowing it likely to be sold/used for a medicinal purpose as if unadulterated -- punishable with up to one year's imprisonment plus fine up to five thousand rupees, double the maximum for the parallel food-adulteration offence under Section 274.
glossary.selling or dispensing adulterated drugs: Section 277 BNS: knowingly selling, offering for sale, issuing from a dispensary, or causing the use of an adulterated drug for medicinal purposes as if unadulterated -- punishable with up to six months' imprisonment plus fine up to five thousand rupees, the selling/dispensing-side mirror of Section 276.
glossary.selling a drug as a different drug or pr: Section 278 BNS: knowingly selling, offering for sale, or dispensing a drug or medical preparation as if it were a different drug or preparation -- a mislabelling/misrepresentation offence distinct from adulteration, punishable identically to selling adulterated drugs under Section 277.
glossary.voluntarily fouling water of a public sp: Section 279 BNS: voluntarily corrupting or fouling the water of a public spring or reservoir so as to render it less fit for its ordinary use, punishable with up to six months' imprisonment plus fine up to five thousand rupees -- a relatively low harm threshold ('less fit', not unusable) reflecting its preventive, public-health-protective character.
glossary.voluntarily vitiating the atmosphere to: Section 280 BNS: voluntarily vitiating the atmosphere in a place so as to make it noxious to the health of people generally dwelling, working, or passing by nearby -- an early air-pollution offence punishable only with a fine up to one thousand rupees, the lightest (fine-only, no imprisonment option) of the chapter's environmental-nuisance offences.
glossary.rash or negligent driving or riding on a: Section 281 BNS: driving a vehicle or riding on a public way in a manner so rash or negligent as to endanger human life or be likely to cause hurt or injury, punishable with up to six months' imprisonment plus fine up to one thousand rupees -- the land-transport counterpart to Section 282's rash-vessel-navigation offence.
glossary.rash or negligent navigation of a vessel: Section 282 BNS: navigating a vessel so rashly or negligently as to endanger human life or be likely to cause hurt or injury, punishable with up to six months' imprisonment plus fine up to ten thousand rupees -- the water-transport mirror of Section 281, with a tenfold higher fine ceiling reflecting the generally higher stakes of reckless vessel navigation.
glossary.exhibiting a false light mark or buoy to: Section 283 BNS: exhibiting a false light, mark, or buoy, intending or knowing it likely to mislead a navigator, punishable with up to seven years' imprisonment plus a mandatory minimum fine of ten thousand rupees -- by far the heaviest offence in the maritime-safety cluster, reflecting the catastrophic shipwreck/mass-casualty risk this conduct creates.
glossary.conveying a person for hire in an unsafe: Section 284 BNS: knowingly or negligently conveying, or causing to be conveyed, a person by water for hire in a vessel so unsafe or overloaded as to endanger that person's life, punishable with up to six months' imprisonment plus fine up to five thousand rupees -- protects paying passengers, distinct from Section 282's rash-navigation offence which targets reckless operation rather than inherent unsafety.
glossary.causing danger obstruction or injury in: Section 285 BNS: a fine-only offence (up to five thousand rupees) covering both acts and omissions -- doing an act, or omitting to properly manage property in one's possession or charge, so as to cause danger, obstruction, or injury to anyone in a public way or public line of navigation; functions as a broad catch-all beneath the more specific negligence offences of Sections 286-291.
glossary.rash or negligent act with a poisonous s: The active-conduct limb of Section 286 BNS: doing an act with a poisonous substance in a manner so rash or negligent as to endanger human life or be likely to cause hurt or injury, punishable with up to six months' imprisonment plus fine up to five thousand rupees.
glossary.negligent omission to safeguard a poison: The passive-omission limb of Section 286 BNS: knowingly or negligently omitting to take precautions sufficient to guard against probable danger to human life from a poisonous substance in one's possession, punished identically to the active-conduct limb -- the first of six structurally parallel 'negligent conduct with respect to X' offences spanning Sections 286-291.
glossary.rash or negligent act with fire or combu: The active-conduct limb of Section 287 BNS: doing an act with fire or combustible matter in a manner so rash or negligent as to endanger human life or be likely to cause hurt or injury, punishable with up to six months' imprisonment plus fine up to two thousand rupees -- a lower fine ceiling than the parallel poisonous-substance offence.
glossary.negligent omission to safeguard fire or: The passive-omission limb of Section 287 BNS: knowingly or negligently omitting sufficient precautions with fire or combustible matter in one's possession to guard against probable danger to human life, punished identically to the active-conduct limb of the same section.
glossary.rash or negligent act with an explosive: The active-conduct limb of Section 288 BNS: doing an act with an explosive substance in a manner so rash or negligent as to endanger human life or be likely to cause hurt or injury, punishable with up to six months' imprisonment plus fine up to five thousand rupees -- covers negligence only; deliberate misuse of explosives to cause harm falls under heavier body/property offences elsewhere in the Sanhita.
glossary.negligent omission to safeguard an explo: The passive-omission limb of Section 288 BNS: knowingly or negligently omitting sufficient precautions with an explosive substance in one's possession to guard against probable danger to human life, punished identically to the active-conduct limb of the same section.
glossary.rash or negligent act with machinery: The active-conduct limb of Section 289 BNS: doing an act with machinery in a manner so rash or negligent as to endanger human life or be likely to cause hurt or injury, punishable with up to six months' imprisonment plus fine up to five thousand rupees.
glossary.negligent omission to safeguard machiner: The passive-omission limb of Section 289 BNS: knowingly or negligently omitting sufficient precautions with machinery in one's possession or under one's care to guard against probable danger to human life -- the 'or under his care' wording extends this slightly beyond strict legal possession, unlike the parallel poison/fire/explosive provisions.
glossary.negligent omission to safeguard against: Section 290 BNS: a person pulling down, repairing, or constructing a building who knowingly or negligently omits measures sufficient to guard against the probable danger of the building (or part of it) falling, punishable with up to six months' imprisonment plus fine up to five thousand rupees -- unlike Sections 286-289, this has only a single omission-based limb, with no separate rash-act limb.

Section 291 BNS, closing the negligence-offence cluster: knowingly or negligently omitting measures sufficient to guard against probable danger to human life, or probable grievous hurt, from an animal in one's possession, punishable with up to six months' imprisonment plus fine up to five thousand rupees -- like Section 290, a single omission-based limb with no separate rash-act limb.
glossary.residual punishment for public nuisance: Section 292 BNS: the catch-all fine-only punishment (up to one thousand rupees) for conduct meeting the Section 270 public-nuisance definition but not already specifically punished elsewhere in the Sanhita -- always check the more targeted provisions (Sections 271-291 and others) first.
glossary.repeating or continuing a nuisance after: Section 293 BNS: repeating or continuing a public nuisance after being enjoined to stop by a public servant with lawful authority to issue such an injunction, punishable with up to six months' simple imprisonment plus fine up to five thousand rupees -- far heavier than Section 292's plain fine-only residual punishment, reflecting the added seriousness of defying a specific lawful official order.
glossary.obscenity test for books and other objec: Section 294(1) BNS: material is deemed obscene if it is lascivious, appeals to the prurient interest, or if its effect (or the effect of any one item within a composite work), taken as a whole, tends to deprave and corrupt persons likely to read, see, or hear it -- expressly extended to cover display of content in electronic form, not just physical books or objects.
glossary.selling distributing or circulating obsc: Section 294(2) BNS: the broad conduct offence built on the sub-section (1) obscenity test -- selling, hiring, distributing, publicly exhibiting, circulating, producing, possessing for those purposes, importing/exporting/conveying, profiting from such a business, advertising such material, or attempting any of the above, punishable up to two years (first conviction) escalating to five years (second or subsequent conviction), subject to public-good and religious-use exceptions.
glossary.public-good and bona fide religious-use: The Exception to Section 294 BNS: material whose publication is proved justified as being for the public good on grounds of science, literature, art, learning, or other objects of general concern, or kept/used bona fide for religious purposes, falls outside the obscenity offence entirely -- as do representations on protected ancient monuments or on temples/idol-conveyance cars used for religious purposes.
glossary.selling or distributing an obscene objec: Section 295 BNS: the child-protection escalation of Section 294 -- selling, hiring, distributing, exhibiting, or circulating (or attempting) a Section-294-obscene object specifically to a child, punishable up to three years (first conviction) escalating to seven years (second or subsequent conviction), both tiers heavier than the general Section 294 obscenity offence.
glossary.obscene act in a public place: The first limb of Section 296 BNS: doing an obscene act in a public place to the annoyance of others, punishable with up to three months' imprisonment plus fine up to one thousand rupees -- targets live public conduct, distinct from Section 294's offences concerning obscene material/objects.
glossary.obscene song ballad or words in or near: The second limb of Section 296 BNS: singing, reciting, or uttering an obscene song, ballad, or words in or near a public place, to the annoyance of others, punished identically to the obscene-act limb of the same section -- the 'to the annoyance of others' requirement is an operative element the prosecution must prove.
glossary.keeping an office for an unauthorised lo: Section 297(1) BNS, closing Chapter XV: keeping any office or place for drawing a lottery that is neither a State lottery nor one authorised by the State Government, punishable with up to six months' imprisonment, fine, or both -- State-run or State-authorised lotteries are entirely outside this prohibition.
glossary.publishing a proposal tied to the drawin: Section 297(2) BNS: publishing any proposal to pay a sum, deliver goods, or do/forbear from doing anything for a person's benefit, contingent on the drawing of a ticket, lot, number, or figure in an unauthorised lottery -- a fine-only offence (up to five thousand rupees) targeting promoters/advertisers rather than the office-keeping operator covered by sub-section (1).
glossary.destroying damaging or defiling a place: Section 298 BNS, opening Chapter XVI: destroying, damaging, or defiling a place of worship or an object held sacred by any class of persons, with intention of insulting that class's religion or knowledge that the class is likely to consider it an insult, punishable with up to two years' imprisonment, fine, or both -- the knowledge-based alternative means reckless disregard of foreseeable religious-insult impact suffices just as much as deliberate intent.
glossary.deliberate and malicious intention to ou: The demanding mens rea threshold in Section 299 BNS: mere offence-giving is not enough -- the accused must have deliberately and maliciously intended to outrage the religious feelings of a class of citizens, a standard courts scrutinise closely before allowing prosecutions to proceed, particularly against artistic, academic, or satirical expression.
glossary.insulting religion or religious beliefs: The conduct element of Section 299 BNS: insulting, or attempting to insult, the religion or religious beliefs of a class of Indian citizens by spoken or written words, signs, visible representations, electronic means, or otherwise, punishable with up to three years' imprisonment, fine, or both when paired with the section's deliberate-and-malicious-intent requirement.
glossary.voluntarily disturbing a lawful religiou: Section 300 BNS: voluntarily causing disturbance to an assembly lawfully engaged in religious worship or religious ceremonies, punishable with up to one year's imprisonment, fine, or both -- the 'lawfully engaged' qualifier means the protected assembly's religious activity must itself be lawful.
glossary.trespassing on a place of worship sepulc: A limb of Section 301 BNS: committing trespass in a place of worship, a place of sepulchre, or a place set apart for funeral rites or as a depository for remains of the dead, done with intent to wound feelings or insult religion (or knowledge that such wounding/insult is likely), punishable with up to one year's imprisonment, fine, or both.
glossary.offering indignity to a human corpse: A further limb of Section 301 BNS: offering any indignity to a human corpse, done with intent to wound feelings or insult religion (or knowledge of that likelihood), punished identically to the section's trespass and funeral-disturbance limbs.
glossary.disturbing persons assembled for funeral: The final limb of Section 301 BNS: causing disturbance to persons assembled for the performance of funeral ceremonies, done with intent to wound feelings or insult religion (or knowledge of that likelihood) -- all three Section 301 limbs share this common mental-state requirement.
glossary.uttering words or making sounds gestures: Section 302 BNS, closing Chapter XVI: with deliberate intention of wounding a specific person's religious feelings, uttering a word, making a sound in their hearing, making a gesture in their sight, or placing an object in their sight, punishable with up to one year's imprisonment, fine, or both -- the individual-targeted sibling of Section 299's class-wide offence, capped lower (one year vs. three) because it protects one person rather than a class.
glossary.theft: Section 303(1) BNS, opening Chapter XVII: dishonestly taking any movable property out of the possession of any person without that person's consent, and moving it in order to such taking -- the foundational property offence against which snatching, aggravated theft, theft by clerks/servants, and theft-after-preparation are all defined as variants or aggravations; base punishment up to three years' imprisonment, fine, or both, with a mandatory one-to-five-year rigorous imprisonment band on a repeat conviction, subject to a community-service proviso for first-time low-value theft on restitution.
glossary.dishonest intention as the core of theft: The mens rea that separates theft from an innocent taking under Section 303 BNS -- the taking must be 'dishonest' (intending wrongful gain to oneself or wrongful loss to another), which is why the section's illustrations repeatedly contrast a genuine, good-faith claim of right or an honest mistake (no offence) against a knowing, deliberate appropriation after the true position becomes clear (theft).
glossary.movable property capable of being attach: Explanation 1 to Section 303 BNS: a thing attached to the earth is not ordinarily 'movable property' and so cannot be stolen as it stands, but the moment it is severed from the earth it becomes movable property capable of being the subject of theft -- severance is itself treated as part of the act of taking under Explanation 2.
glossary.moving property in order to taking: Explanations 2-5 to Section 303 BNS collectively define what counts as the 'moving' element of theft: a thing is moved by the very act of severing it from the earth; by removing an obstacle so as to obtain access to it, or by separating it from anything to which it is fastened; and causing an animal to move counts as moving everything that the animal's motion in turn moves -- each extending the mechanical scope of what 'taking' can mean beyond simple manual lifting.
glossary.consent express or implied for theft pur: Explanation 5 to Section 303 BNS: the consent that negates theft may be express or implied, given by the person in possession, or by a person having authority either express or implied to give consent on the possessor's behalf -- several of the section's illustrations turn on whether the taker honestly but mistakenly believed such implied consent existed.
glossary.snatching as a form of theft: Section 304(1) BNS: theft is 'snatching' if the offender, in order to commit theft, suddenly or quickly or forcibly seizes, secures, or grabs movable property from any person or their possession -- a named sub-species of theft carrying a mandatory fine in addition to up to three years' imprisonment, distinguished from base theft by the element of sudden/forcible seizure rather than a stealthy taking.
glossary.sudden quick or forcible seizing to comm: The defining operative element of snatching under Section 304 BNS -- the seizure of property must be sudden, quick, or forcible, which is what separates this named offence (carrying a mandatory fine on top of imprisonment) from an ordinary, unobserved theft under Section 303.
glossary.theft in a dwelling or property-custody: One of the five aggravating contexts in Section 305 BNS: committing theft in a building, tent, or vessel which is used as a human dwelling, or used for the custody of property, punishable with up to seven years' imprisonment plus fine -- markedly heavier than base theft because the location itself signals a greater invasion of security and privacy.
glossary.theft of or from a means of transport: A second aggravating context in Section 305 BNS: committing theft of a means of transportation, or of property contained in such a means of transportation, or while that means of transportation is actually carrying property, punishable with up to seven years' imprisonment plus fine alongside the section's other four aggravated-location limbs.
glossary.theft of an idol or icon from a place of: A third aggravating context in Section 305 BNS: committing theft of an idol or icon from any place set apart for worship, punishable with up to seven years' imprisonment plus fine -- reflecting heightened protection for objects of religious veneration, distinct from Chapter XVI's religion-insult offences which protect feelings rather than property.
glossary.theft of government or local-authority p: The final aggravating context listed in Section 305 BNS: committing theft of property belonging to the Government or a local authority, punishable with up to seven years' imprisonment plus fine on the same footing as the section's dwelling, transport, and place-of-worship aggravations.
glossary.theft by a clerk or servant of the maste: Section 306 BNS: theft committed by a clerk or servant of movable property in the possession of their master, punishable with up to seven years' imprisonment plus fine -- the breach-of-trust-adjacent aggravation targeting the employment relationship, pitched at the same seven-year ceiling as Section 305's location-based aggravations.
glossary.theft preceded by preparation for causin: Section 307 BNS, the most severely punished theft variant: committing theft after making preparation for causing death, hurt, or wrongful restraint, or fear of death/hurt/wrongful restraint, to any person in order to the committing of the theft, or in order to the effecting of an escape after the theft, or in order to the retaining of stolen property, punishable with up to ten years' rigorous imprisonment plus fine -- illustrated by carrying a loaded pistol in case of resistance and posting companions to restrain the victim if needed, showing that even unexecuted contingent preparation for violence is enough to trigger this enhanced punishment.
glossary.community service for first-time low-val: The proviso to Section 303(2) BNS: where a person is convicted of theft for the first time and the value of the stolen property is less than five thousand rupees, and the property is restored or returned, the court may impose community service in lieu of other punishment -- a rehabilitative off-ramp available only on a first conviction and only below the value threshold, unlike the mandatory one-to-five-year enhancement that applies on a second or subsequent theft conviction.
glossary.extortion: Section 308(1) BNS, opening the 'Of extortion' sub-chapter: intentionally putting a person in fear of any injury to them or another, and thereby dishonestly inducing them to deliver property, a valuable security, or a document convertible into one -- the base definition on which the section's graduated seven-sub-section punishment ladder, and the robbery/dacoity provisions that build on extortion, both depend.
glossary.putting a person in fear of injury to di: The core conduct element of extortion under Section 308(1) BNS -- the fear induced must be of 'any injury' (a deliberately broad term covering reputational, economic, physical, or other harm, as shown by the section's defamatory-libel and wrongful-confinement illustrations) and must dishonestly induce the actual delivery of property, a valuable security, or a convertible document.
glossary.tiered extortion punishment escalating w: Sub-sections (2)-(7) of Section 308 BNS build a graduated punishment ladder on top of the base extortion definition: up to seven years for ordinary extortion, down to two years for merely putting/attempting to put someone in fear of 'any injury' in order to extortion, up to ten years where the fear used (or attempted) is of death or grievous hurt, and up to ten years again where the fear used (or attempted) is of a false accusation of a death/life/ten-year offence -- the ladder sorts punishment by both the gravity of the threatened harm and whether the extortion was completed or only attempted.
glossary.robbery as aggravated theft or aggravate: Section 309(1) BNS's foundational premise: robbery is not an independent offence but always either theft or extortion that has been aggravated by violence, restraint, or fear of instant harm -- sub-sections (2) and (3) then separately define the theft-route and extortion-route versions of this aggravation.
glossary.theft aggravated into robbery by violenc: Section 309(2) BNS: theft becomes robbery when, in order to commit the theft, while committing it, or in carrying away (or attempting to carry away) the stolen property, the offender voluntarily causes or attempts to cause death, hurt, or wrongful restraint, or fear of instant death, instant hurt, or instant wrongful restraint -- illustrated by physically holding a victim down while taking their money and jewels.
glossary.extortion aggravated into robbery by the: Section 309(3) BNS: extortion becomes robbery when the offender, physically present before the victim, induces immediate (not future) delivery of the extorted thing by putting the victim in fear of instant death, instant hurt, or instant wrongful restraint -- the explanation clarifies 'presence' as being sufficiently near to instil that instant fear, and illustration (d) shows that a ransom threat against a child already removed from the scene is extortion but not robbery, since the threatened harm is not instant.
glossary.enhanced robbery punishment for offences: Section 309(4) BNS: base robbery carries up to ten years' rigorous imprisonment plus fine, but that ceiling rises to fourteen years if the robbery is committed on the highway between sunset and sunrise -- a time-and-location-based aggravation reflecting the heightened danger of nighttime highway robbery.
glossary.joint liability for hurt voluntarily cau: Section 309(6) BNS: if any person voluntarily causes hurt while committing or attempting robbery, both that person and every other person jointly concerned in committing or attempting the robbery are punished with life imprisonment or up to ten years' rigorous imprisonment plus fine -- a constructive-liability provision extending punishment to the whole group, not just the one who actually caused the hurt.
glossary.dacoity as robbery by five or more perso: Section 310(1) BNS: robbery becomes dacoity purely by headcount -- whenever five or more persons conjointly commit or attempt a robbery, or the combined total of those committing/attempting it plus those present and aiding reaches five or more, every one of them is said to commit dacoity, regardless of each individual's specific role.
glossary.constructive liability of every dacoity: Section 310(3) BNS, the sharpest constructive-liability provision in the robbery/dacoity cluster: if any one of five or more persons conjointly committing dacoity commits murder in the course of it, every one of those persons -- not just the actual killer -- is punished with death, life imprisonment, or rigorous imprisonment of not less than ten years, plus fine.
glossary.preparation for committing dacoity as a: Section 310(4) BNS: making any preparation for committing dacoity is independently punishable with up to ten years' rigorous imprisonment plus fine, regardless of whether the dacoity itself is ever attempted or completed -- criminalising an early stage of the offence on its own.
glossary.mere assembly of five or more persons fo: Section 310(5) BNS: being one of five or more persons assembled for the purpose of committing dacoity is itself punishable with up to seven years' rigorous imprisonment plus fine, a step even earlier than the preparation offence in sub-section (4), targeting the group's mere assembly with that shared purpose.
glossary.belonging to a gang habitually committin: Section 310(6) BNS: belonging to a gang of persons associated for the purpose of habitually committing dacoity is punishable with life imprisonment or up to ten years' rigorous imprisonment plus fine -- the most severely punished of the dacoity-cluster's preparatory/associative offences, reflecting habitual gang membership as nearly as grave as the completed offence itself.
glossary.mandatory minimum sentence for robbery o: Section 311 BNS: where the offender uses a deadly weapon, causes grievous hurt, or attempts to cause death or grievous hurt while committing robbery or dacoity, the sentence cannot be less than seven years -- a mandatory floor layered on top of the ordinary robbery (Section 309) and dacoity (Section 310) sentencing ranges, not a new offence in itself.
glossary.mandatory minimum sentence for attemptin: Section 312 BNS: merely being armed with a deadly weapon at the time of attempting robbery or dacoity triggers the same mandatory seven-year minimum sentence as Section 311, without needing proof that the weapon was used or that any hurt was caused or attempted -- armed presence during the attempt alone suffices.
glossary.belonging to a gang habitually committin: Section 313 BNS, closing the 'Of robbery and dacoity' sub-chapter: belonging to a gang associated for habitually committing theft or robbery -- expressly excluding gangs of dacoits, who fall under Section 310(6)'s heavier punishment instead -- is punishable with up to seven years' rigorous imprisonment plus fine, sorting gang-membership liability by the gravity of what the gang habitually does.
glossary.dishonest misappropriation of movable pr: Section 314 BNS, opening the 'Of criminal misappropriation of property' sub-chapter: dishonestly misappropriating or converting to one's own use any movable property, punishable with a mandatory minimum six months rising to a maximum of two years plus fine -- distinguished from theft (no prior possession needed, but a non-consensual taking is) and from criminal breach of trust (which requires prior entrustment) by typically beginning with innocent or lawful possession that later turns dishonest.
glossary.temporary misappropriation still countin: Explanation 1 to Section 314 BNS: a dishonest misappropriation 'for a time only' still falls within the section -- illustrated by pledging a found Government promissory note with a banker while intending to restore it to the true owner later, which is nonetheless an offence despite the intended eventual return.
glossary.honest-finder exception for property not: Explanation 2 to Section 314 BNS: a person who finds property not in anyone's possession, and takes it to protect or restore it to the owner, does not dishonestly misappropriate it and commits no offence -- unless they later appropriate it to their own use despite knowing or having the means of discovering the owner, or before using reasonable means/time to find and notify the owner.
glossary.reasonable means and reasonable time to: A sub-clause of Explanation 2 to Section 314 BNS: what counts as 'reasonable means' or 'reasonable time' for a finder of property to attempt to locate and notify the true owner before appropriation becomes dishonest is not fixed by the statute but left as a question of fact for each case -- the finder need not know the specific owner's identity, only must not believe the property is their own or genuinely believe the real owner cannot be found.
glossary.misappropriating a deceased person's pro: Section 315 BNS: dishonestly misappropriating or converting to one's own use property known to have been in a deceased person's possession at the time of death, where it has not since reached anyone legally entitled to possess it (such as an heir or executor), punishable with up to three years plus fine -- a specialised misappropriation variant targeting the vulnerable window immediately following a death.
glossary.enhanced punishment where the offender w: The aggravated limb of Section 315 BNS: where the offender who misappropriates a deceased person's property was, at the time of that person's death, employed by them as a clerk or servant, the punishment rises from three years to up to seven years -- mirroring Section 306's and Section 316(4)'s parallel enhancement of punishment where the wrongdoer exploited an employment-based position of trust.
glossary.criminal breach of trust: Section 316(1) BNS, opening the 'Of criminal breach of trust' sub-chapter: committed by a person who, being entrusted with property or dominion over property, dishonestly misappropriates or converts it to their own use, or dishonestly uses/disposes of it in violation of a legal direction or a contract (express or implied) governing the trust, or wilfully allows another person to do so -- distinguished from Section 314 misappropriation by the essential prior element of entrustment by another person.
glossary.deemed entrustment and dishonest use for: Explanations 1 and 2 to Section 316 BNS: an employer who deducts an employee's Provident Fund/Family Pension Fund or Employees' State Insurance contribution from wages is deemed to have been entrusted with that amount, and a default in remitting it to the relevant fund is deemed a dishonest use of the entrusted money in violation of a legal direction -- a statutory fiction that brings wage-deduction defaults squarely within criminal breach of trust without needing to separately prove entrustment or dishonest intent in the ordinary sense.
glossary.enhanced criminal breach of trust by a c: Section 316(3) BNS: criminal breach of trust committed by a person entrusted with property in their capacity as a carrier, wharfinger, or warehouse-keeper is punishable with up to seven years' imprisonment plus fine, higher than the five-year base offence in sub-section (2), reflecting the elevated trust society places in custodial transport/storage roles.

Section 316(4) BNS: criminal breach of trust committed by a clerk or servant (or person employed as one) in respect of property entrusted to them in that capacity is punishable with up to seven years' imprisonment plus fine -- the same elevated ceiling as the carrier/wharfinger/warehouse-keeper aggravation in sub-section (3), and consistent with the employment-based enhancements seen throughout this chapter (Sections 306, 315).
glossary.most severe enhancement for criminal bre: Section 316(5) BNS, the heaviest tier in the criminal-breach-of-trust sub-chapter: criminal breach of trust committed by a person entrusted with property in their capacity as a public servant, or in the way of business as a banker, merchant, factor, broker, attorney, or agent, is punishable with imprisonment for life or up to ten years plus fine -- reflecting the especially high degree of public and commercial trust reposed in these roles.
glossary.stolen property definition spanning thef: Section 317(1) BNS's foundational definition, opening the 'Of receiving stolen property' sub-chapter: 'stolen property' covers property whose possession was transferred by theft, extortion, robbery, or cheating, and property that has been criminally misappropriated or is the subject of criminal breach of trust -- wherever in the world that underlying offence occurred -- giving the receiving-offences that follow a deliberately wide net of qualifying source crimes.
glossary.property ceasing to be stolen once it re: The closing qualifier of Section 317(1) BNS: property only remains 'stolen property' for the purposes of this sub-chapter until it comes into the possession of a person legally entitled to possess it -- once restored to a rightful possessor, a subsequent receiver dealing with it falls outside this section entirely.
glossary.dishonestly receiving or retaining prope: Section 317(2) BNS, the base receiving-stolen-property offence: dishonestly receiving or retaining any stolen property, knowing or having reason to believe it to be stolen, punishable with up to three years' imprisonment, fine, or both -- 'reason to believe' sets a lower threshold than actual knowledge, satisfied by circumstances that would lead a reasonable person to that belief.
glossary.enhanced punishment for receiving proper: Section 317(3) BNS: dishonestly receiving or retaining property known/believed to have been obtained through dacoity, or dishonestly receiving property known/believed to be stolen from a person known/believed to belong (or to have belonged) to a gang of dacoits, is punished far more heavily than ordinary receiving -- life imprisonment or up to ten years' rigorous imprisonment plus fine -- reflecting the greater societal harm of financially sustaining organised dacoit gangs.
glossary.habitually receiving or dealing in stole: Section 317(4) BNS: habitually receiving or dealing in property known or believed to be stolen is punished at the same elevated level as dacoity-linked receiving -- life imprisonment or up to ten years' imprisonment plus fine -- targeting repeat/professional fences rather than one-off receivers, who fall under the lighter sub-section (2).
glossary.voluntarily assisting in concealing disp: Section 317(5) BNS: voluntarily assisting in concealing, disposing of, or making away with property known or believed to be stolen is a distinct offence from receiving/retaining itself, punishable with up to three years' imprisonment, fine, or both -- covering accomplices who help a thief or receiver dispose of or hide stolen goods without necessarily taking possession of the property themselves.
glossary.cheating by deception inducing delivery: Section 318(1) BNS, opening the 'Of cheating' sub-chapter: deceiving a person and thereby fraudulently or dishonestly inducing them to deliver property or consent to another retaining property, OR intentionally inducing them to do or omit something they otherwise would not, where that act or omission causes or is likely to cause damage or harm to body, mind, reputation, or property -- the property-delivery and harmful-act/omission limbs are alternative routes to the same offence.
glossary.dishonest concealment of facts as a form: The Explanation to Section 318 BNS: a dishonest concealment of facts counts as 'deception' for cheating purposes just as much as an affirmative false statement -- illustrated by illustration (i), where failing to disclose a prior sale of an estate before selling/mortgaging it a second time constitutes cheating through concealment rather than through any spoken falsehood.
glossary.cheating distinguished from a mere civil: The core timing principle drawn from illustration (g) to Section 318 BNS: cheating requires the dishonest intent (e.g., not intending to perform, or not intending to pay) to exist at the moment the inducement is made -- if the promisor genuinely intended to perform at that time and only later broke the contract, the matter is a civil wrong only, not a criminal cheating offence.
glossary.enhanced cheating punishment where the o: Section 318(3) BNS: where the offender cheats with knowledge that they are likely to cause wrongful loss to a person whose interest in the transaction they were bound, by law or by a legal contract, to protect, the punishment rises from the base three years (sub-section 2) to up to five years, fine, or both -- targeting cheating that breaches a pre-existing fiduciary or protective duty.
glossary.enhanced cheating punishment where prope: Section 318(4) BNS, the heaviest cheating tier: where the cheating actually dishonestly induces the victim to deliver property, or to make, alter, or destroy the whole or part of a valuable security or a document signed/sealed and capable of being converted into one, the punishment rises to up to seven years plus fine -- reserved for cheating that achieves its intended material result, not merely the attempt.
glossary.cheating by personation: Section 319(1) BNS: a named sub-species of cheating committed by pretending to be some other person, knowingly substituting one person for another, or representing oneself or another as a person other than they really are, punishable with up to five years' imprisonment, fine, or both -- a heavier ceiling than Section 318's base three-year cheating offence, reflecting the additional layer of fraud involved in fabricating or borrowing an identity.
glossary.personation offence applying whether the: The Explanation to Section 319 BNS: cheating by personation is committed whether the individual being impersonated is a real person (living or, per illustration (b), even deceased) or a wholly imaginary person -- the offence does not depend on the impersonated identity actually existing.
glossary.removing concealing or transferring prop: Section 320 BNS, opening the 'Of fraudulent deeds and dispositions of property' sub-chapter: dishonestly or fraudulently removing, concealing, delivering, or transferring property without adequate consideration, intending (or knowing it likely) to prevent that property's lawful distribution among creditors, punishable with a mandatory minimum six months rising to two years, fine, or both -- a genuine sale at fair value falls outside this section since the 'without adequate consideration' element would be absent.
glossary.preventing a debt or demand due to onese: Section 321 BNS: dishonestly or fraudulently preventing a debt or demand owed to oneself or another person from being made legally available to pay one's own debts or that other person's debts, punishable with up to two years, fine, or both -- the mirror image of Section 320, targeting suppression of an incoming receivable rather than concealment of existing property, but sharing the same intent-to-defeat-creditors core.
glossary.executing a deed of transfer with a fals: Section 322 BNS: dishonestly or fraudulently signing, executing, or becoming a party to a deed or instrument purporting to transfer or charge property, where that document falsely states the consideration for the transfer/charge or falsely identifies who is really intended to benefit from it, punishable with up to three years, fine, or both -- a documentary-fraud offence targeting sham or misleading paperwork rather than the underlying asset-concealment conduct itself.
glossary.concealing or removing one's own or anot: Section 323 BNS, closing the 'Of fraudulent deeds and dispositions of property' sub-chapter: a residual offence covering dishonestly/fraudulently concealing or removing property (one's own or another's), assisting in such concealment/removal, or dishonestly releasing a demand or claim one is entitled to, punishable with up to three years, fine, or both -- its 'releasing a demand or claim' limb uniquely covers a debtor who forgives money owed to them specifically to keep it out of their creditors' reach.
glossary.mischief as destroying or injuriously af: Section 324(1) BNS, opening the 'Of mischief' sub-chapter: causing the destruction of property, or a change in property or its situation that destroys/diminishes its value or utility or injuriously affects it, with intent to cause (or knowledge of likelihood of causing) wrongful loss or damage to the public or any person -- the foundational property-damage offence beneath the chapter's animal, water-supply/fire/explosive, rail/vessel, and vessel-grounding aggravations.
glossary.mischief not requiring intent to harm th: Explanation 1 to Section 324 BNS: it is not essential that the offender intend loss or damage to the property's actual owner -- it suffices that they intend, or know themselves likely, to cause wrongful loss or damage to any person by injuring property, whether or not that property belongs to that person; illustration (f) (scuttling a ship to harm a lender who merely holds a bottomry interest in it, not the owner) demonstrates this breadth.
glossary.mischief committable against one's own o: Explanation 2 to Section 324 BNS: mischief may be committed by an act affecting property belonging to the person who commits the act, or to that person and others jointly -- illustrated by an insured shipowner scuttling their own ship to defraud underwriters, and a joint owner shooting a jointly-owned horse to cause wrongful loss to the co-owner.
glossary.value-tiered mischief punishment escalat: Sub-sections (2)-(5) of Section 324 BNS build a monetary-threshold sentencing ladder on the base mischief offence: six months where no loss/damage results, up to one year where actual loss/damage is caused (including to Government or local-authority property), up to two years for loss between twenty thousand and one lakh rupees, and up to five years for loss of one lakh rupees or more.
glossary.mischief committed after preparation for: Section 324(6) BNS: committing mischief having made preparation for causing death, hurt, or wrongful restraint (or fear of any of these) to any person is punished with up to five years plus mandatory fine -- the mischief-specific counterpart to Section 307's parallel enhancement for theft preceded by preparation for violence.
glossary.mischief by killing poisoning maiming or: Section 325 BNS: a named, aggravated mischief variant targeting living animals -- killing, poisoning, maiming, or rendering useless any animal, punishable with up to five years, fine, or both, a significantly heavier ceiling than Section 324's base mischief bands, reflecting the distinct harm of mischief directed at a living creature.
glossary.mischief by diminishing the water supply: Section 326(a) BNS: committing mischief by doing any act which causes, or which the offender knows to be likely to cause, a diminution of the supply of water for agricultural purposes, or for human/animal food or drink, or for cleanliness, or for carrying on any manufacture, punishable with up to five years, fine, or both -- the first of seven aggravated-mischief limbs in Section 326, each keyed to a distinct public or safety-critical target.
glossary.mischief by making a public road bridge: Section 326(b) BNS: committing mischief by doing any act which renders, or is known to be likely to render, any public road, bridge, navigable river, or navigable channel (natural or artificial) impassable or less safe for travelling or conveying property, punishable with up to five years, fine, or both.
glossary.mischief by causing inundation or obstru: Section 326(c) BNS: committing mischief by doing any act which causes, or is known to be likely to cause, an inundation or an obstruction to any public drainage, attended with injury or damage, punishable with up to five years, fine, or both.
glossary.mischief by destroying or moving a navig: Section 326(d) BNS: committing mischief by destroying or moving any sign or signal used for the navigation of rail, aircraft, or ship, or any other thing placed as a guide for navigators, or by any act rendering such a sign or signal less useful as a guide, punishable with up to seven years, fine, or both -- a heavier ceiling than the water-supply, road/bridge, and drainage limbs, reflecting the transport-safety stakes.
glossary.mischief by destroying or moving a publi: Section 326(e) BNS: committing mischief by destroying or moving any land-mark fixed by the authority of a public servant, or by any act rendering such land-mark less useful as such, punishable with up to one year, fine, or both -- the lightest of the seven limbs in Section 326.
glossary.mischief by fire or explosive substance: Section 326(f) BNS: committing mischief by fire or any explosive substance, intending to cause, or knowing it likely that it will cause, damage to any property including agricultural produce, punishable with up to seven years and mandatory fine.

Section 326(g) BNS: committing mischief by fire or any explosive substance, intending to cause, or knowing it likely that it will cause, the destruction of any building ordinarily used as a place of worship, as a human dwelling, or as a place for the custody of property, punishable with life imprisonment or up to ten years plus mandatory fine -- the heaviest of Section 326's seven limbs, reflecting the direct threat to human life and safety from fire/explosives against occupied or sacred buildings.
glossary.mischief intending to destroy or make un: Section 327(1) BNS: committing mischief to any rail, aircraft, decked vessel, or vessel of twenty tons burden or upwards, intending to destroy or render it unsafe, or knowing it likely that this will result, punishable with up to ten years plus fine.
