The consideration is for that person concealing an offence, screening an offender, or not proceeding to bring them to legal punishment
exceptions_and_qualifications: Sections 250 and 251 do not extend to any case where the offence in question may lawfully be compounded
breakdown.how_to_read: The compounding exception is important: where the law itself permits parties to lawfully settle (compound) an offence, paying or accepting consideration for that lawful settlement is not criminalised under these sections -- only bribery to screen offences that are NOT lawfully compoundable falls within 250-251.

sections.title: Taking gift to help to recover stolen property, etc.
sections.raw_text: Whoever takes or agrees or consents to take any gratification under pretence or on account of helping any person to recover any movable property of which he shall have been deprived by any offence punishable under this Sanhita, shall, unless he uses all means in his power to cause the offender to be apprehended and convicted of the offence, be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.
key_terms: taking a gift to help recover stolen property without pursuing the offender

breakdown.plain_summary: Punishes taking or agreeing to take a gratification under the pretence of helping someone recover movable property of which they were deprived by an offence, unless the person doing so uses all means in their power to get the actual offender apprehended and convicted -- punishable with up to two years' imprisonment, fine, or both.
essential_elements: The accused takes, agrees, or consents to take a gratification under pretence or on account of helping recover movable property lost through an offence
The accused does not use all means in their power to get the offender apprehended and convicted
breakdown.how_to_read: This targets the classic 'recovery agent' scheme -- someone who profits from brokering the return of stolen property without any real effort to bring the actual thief to justice, effectively compounding theft-related offences for personal gain.

sections.title: Harbouring offender who has escaped from custody or whose apprehension has been ordered
sections.raw_text: Whenever any person convicted of or charged with an offence, being in lawful custody for that offence, escapes from such custody, or whenever a public servant, in the exercise of the lawful powers of such public servant, orders a certain person to be apprehended for an offence, whoever, knowing of such escape or order for apprehension, harbours or conceals that person with the intention of preventing him from being apprehended, shall be punished in the manner following, namely:-- (a) if the offence for which the person was in custody or is ordered to be apprehended is punishable with death, he shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine; (b) if the offence is punishable with imprisonment for life or imprisonment for ten years, he shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, with or without fine; (c) if the offence is punishable with imprisonment which may extend to one year and not to ten years, he shall be punished with imprisonment of the description provided for the offence for a term which may extend to one-fourth part of the longest term of the imprisonment provided for such offence, or with fine, or with both. Explanation.--"Offence" in this section includes also any act or omission of which a person is alleged to have been guilty out of India, which, if he had been guilty of it in India, would have been punishable as an offence, and for which he is, under any law relating to extradition, or otherwise, liable to be apprehended or detained in custody in India, and every such act or omission shall, for the purposes of this section, be deemed to be punishable as if the accused person had been guilty of it in India. Exception.--The provisions of this section do not extend to the case in which the harbour or concealment is by the spouse of the person to be apprehended.
key_terms: harbouring an escaped-from-custody or apprehension-ordered person
extradition-linked extraterritorial offence for Section 253

breakdown.plain_summary: A specialised harbouring offence covering two scenarios: harbouring someone who has actually escaped from lawful custody, or harbouring someone a public servant has lawfully ordered to be apprehended, done with intent to prevent apprehension -- same three-tier graduated punishment as Section 249, extended to extradition-relevant extraterritorial acts, with the same spousal exception.
essential_elements: Either a person in lawful custody for an offence has escaped, or a public servant has lawfully ordered a person's apprehension for an offence
The accused knows of that escape or apprehension order
The accused harbours or conceals that person with intention of preventing their apprehension
Punishment tier is keyed to the severity of the underlying offence
exceptions_and_qualifications: This section does not extend to harbouring or concealment by the spouse of the person to be apprehended
breakdown.how_to_read: Distinguish this from Section 249: Section 249 covers harbouring the original offender generally, while Section 253 covers the more specific scenario of someone who has already escaped custody or is already the subject of a formal apprehension order -- the extradition-linked Explanation also broadens its extraterritorial reach beyond Section 249's list of specific cross-referenced offences.

sections.title: Penalty for harbouring robbers or dacoits
sections.raw_text:
Whoever, knowing or having reason to believe that any persons are about to commit or have recently committed robbery or dacoity, harbours them or any of them, with the intention of facilitating the commission of such robbery or dacoity, or of screening them or any of them from punishment, shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.

Explanation.--For the purposes of this section it is immaterial whether the robbery or dacoity is intended to be committed, or has been committed, within or without India.

Exception.--This provision does not extend to the case in which the harbour is given by the spouse of the offender.
key_terms: harbouring robbers or dacoits
facilitating or screening robbery or dacoity through harbour

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 254 BNS specifically targets harbouring persons connected to robbery or dacoity -- a heavier, specialised version of Section 249's general offender-harbouring offence, reflecting the particular seriousness the Sanhita attaches to organised and violent property crime.
essential_elements: harbouring persons
knowledge or reason to believe those persons are about to commit, or have recently committed, robbery or dacoity
intention to facilitate the robbery/dacoity or to screen the persons from punishment
exceptions_and_qualifications: Immaterial whether the robbery or dacoity is intended within or without India (Explanation).
Does not extend to harbour given by the offender's spouse (Exception).
breakdown.how_to_read: Read this as the robbery/dacoity-specific sibling of Section 249 -- it does not replace Section 249's general harbouring offence but adds a heavier, targeted punishment (up to seven years rigorous imprisonment) for harbouring tied specifically to this especially serious category of property crime.

sections.title: Public servant disobeying direction of law with intent to save person from punishment or property from forfeiture
sections.raw_text: Whoever, being a public servant, knowingly disobeys any direction of the law as to the way in which he is to conduct himself as such public servant, intending thereby to save, or knowing it to be likely that he will thereby save, any person from legal punishment, or subject him to a less punishment than that to which he is liable, or with intent to save, or knowing that he is likely thereby to save, any property from forfeiture or any charge to which it is liable by law, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.
key_terms: public servant disobeying legal direction to save a person from punishment
public servant disobeying legal direction to save property from forfeiture

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 255 BNS targets a public servant who knowingly breaks the rules governing their own official conduct, specifically in order to let a person off the hook or spare property from forfeiture -- opening the public-servant-complicity cluster of Chapter XIV, distinct from false-evidence offences committed by ordinary witnesses or litigants.
essential_elements: accused is a public servant
knowing disobedience of a legal direction as to official conduct
intent (or knowledge of likelihood) to save a person from legal punishment, or reduce the punishment to which they are liable
or, alternatively, intent (or knowledge of likelihood) to save property from forfeiture or a legal charge
breakdown.how_to_read: Note the dual-intent structure: either limb (saving a person from punishment, or saving property from forfeiture) independently completes the offence -- a prosecutor only needs to establish one, not both.

sections.title: Public servant framing incorrect record or writing with intent to save person from punishment or property from forfeiture
sections.raw_text: Whoever, being a public servant, and being as such public servant, charged with the preparation of any record or other writing, frames that record or writing in a manner which he knows to be incorrect, with intent to cause, or knowing it to be likely that he will thereby cause, loss or injury to the public or to any person, or with intent thereby to save, or knowing it to be likely that he will thereby save, any person from legal punishment, or with intent to save, or knowing that he is likely thereby to save, any property from forfeiture or other charge to which it is liable by law, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both.
key_terms: public servant knowingly framing an incorrect official record

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 256 BNS is the record-falsification counterpart to Section 255's conduct-disobedience offence -- a public servant tasked with preparing an official record or writing who deliberately frames it incorrectly, whether to harm someone, to save a person from punishment, or to save property from forfeiture.
essential_elements: accused is a public servant charged with preparing a record or other writing
framing the record/writing in a manner known to be incorrect
intent (or knowledge of likelihood) to cause loss or injury to the public or a person, OR
intent (or knowledge of likelihood) to save a person from legal punishment, OR
intent (or knowledge of likelihood) to save property from forfeiture or a legal charge
breakdown.how_to_read: Three independent intent-limbs are listed disjunctively -- loss/injury, saving a person, or saving property -- any one of which suffices; the three-year maximum here is higher than Section 255's two-year maximum because this section involves affirmative falsification of a record rather than mere disobedience of conduct rules.

sections.title: Public servant in judicial proceeding corruptly making report, etc., contrary to law
sections.raw_text: Whoever, being a public servant, corruptly or maliciously makes or pronounces in any stage of a judicial proceeding, any report, order, verdict, or decision which he knows to be contrary to law, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, or with fine, or with both.
key_terms: public servant corruptly making a report order verdict or decision contrary to law

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 257 BNS targets judicial and quasi-judicial corruption directly -- a public servant who, in any stage of a judicial proceeding, corruptly or maliciously issues a report, order, verdict, or decision they know to be contrary to law, carrying a punishment as severe as the heaviest false-evidence band under Section 229(1).
essential_elements: accused is a public servant
acting in any stage of a judicial proceeding
corruptly or maliciously making or pronouncing a report, order, verdict, or decision
knowledge that the report/order/verdict/decision is contrary to law
breakdown.how_to_read: The 'corruptly or maliciously' plus 'knows to be contrary to law' combination sets a high mens rea bar -- an honest legal error or even a negligent misapplication of law does not suffice; this targets deliberate, bad-faith judicial or quasi-judicial corruption.

sections.title: Commitment for trial or confinement by person having authority who knows that he is acting contrary to law
sections.raw_text: Whoever, being in any office which gives him legal authority to commit persons for trial or to confinement, or to keep persons in confinement, corruptly or maliciously commits any person for trial or to confinement, or keeps any person in confinement, in the exercise of that authority knowing that in so doing he is acting contrary to law, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, or with fine, or with both.
key_terms: corruptly committing or confining a person contrary to law

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 258 BNS is the custody-side companion to Section 257's judgment-side corruption offence -- it targets a person holding legal authority over commitment for trial or confinement who corruptly or maliciously exercises that authority knowing it is contrary to law, equally punishable up to seven years.
essential_elements: accused holds an office with legal authority to commit persons for trial or to confinement, or to keep persons in confinement
corruptly or maliciously committing a person for trial or to confinement, or keeping a person in confinement, in exercise of that authority
knowledge that doing so is contrary to law
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Sections 257 and 258 as a pair covering the two ends of judicial-adjacent authority most susceptible to corrupt abuse -- the decision itself (257) and the physical custody consequences that flow from decisions (258).

sections.title: Intentional omission to apprehend on part of public servant bound to apprehend
sections.raw_text:
Whoever, being a public servant, legally bound as such public servant to apprehend or to keep in confinement any person charged with or liable to be apprehended for an offence, intentionally omits to apprehend such person, or intentionally suffers such person to escape, or intentionally aids such person in escaping or attempting to escape from such confinement, shall be punished--

(a) if the person in relation to whom such omission or escape takes place, is charged with or liable to be apprehended for an offence punishable with death, with imprisonment for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine; or

(b) if the person in relation to whom such omission or escape takes place, is charged with or liable to be apprehended for an offence punishable with imprisonment for life or imprisonment for a term of ten years or upwards, with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, and shall also be liable to fine; or

(c) if the person in relation to whom such omission or escape takes place, is charged with or liable to be apprehended for an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term less than ten years, or if the person was taken into custody on a charge of, or for having been concerned in, a non-cognizable offence, or in execution of any process lawfully issued, with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.
key_terms: intentional omission to apprehend by public servant bound to apprehend
intentionally suffering or aiding escape of a person liable to apprehension

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 259 BNS criminalises a public servant who is legally bound to arrest or detain a person charged with (or liable to be apprehended for) an offence, but who intentionally fails to apprehend them, lets them escape, or helps them escape -- punishment graduated across three tiers depending on the severity of the offence the escapee was charged with or liable for.
essential_elements: accused is a public servant legally bound to apprehend or keep in confinement a person charged with, or liable to be apprehended for, an offence
intentional omission to apprehend, OR intentionally suffering the person to escape, OR intentionally aiding escape or attempted escape

punishment tier set by the severity of the offence the person was charged with/liable for: death-punishable (up to 7 years + fine); life/10+-years-punishable (up to 3 years + fine); lesser or non-cognizable/process-based custody (up to 2 years, fine, or both)
breakdown.how_to_read: This section concerns a person who has not yet been convicted -- merely charged with or liable to be apprehended for an offence; contrast with Section 260, which covers the same conduct but for a person already under sentence or lawfully committed, carrying heavier punishment at each tier.

sections.title: Intentional omission to apprehend on part of public servant bound to apprehend person under sentence or lawfully committed
sections.raw_text:
Whoever, being a public servant, legally bound as such public servant to apprehend or to keep in confinement any person under sentence of a Court of Justice for any offence or lawfully committed to custody, intentionally omits to apprehend such person, or intentionally suffers such person to escape, or intentionally aids such person in escaping or attempting to escape from such confinement, shall be punished--

(a) if the person in relation to whom such omission or escape takes place, is under sentence of death, with imprisonment for life or imprisonment for a term which may extend to fourteen years, and shall also be liable to fine; or

(b) if the person in relation to whom such omission or escape takes place, is under sentence of imprisonment for life, or imprisonment for a term of ten years or upwards, with imprisonment for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine; or

(c) if the person in relation to whom such omission or escape takes place, is under sentence of imprisonment for a term less than ten years or lawfully committed to custody, with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both.
key_terms: intentional omission to apprehend a person under sentence or lawfully committed

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 260 BNS mirrors Section 259's structure but for a more serious category of person -- one already under a Court's sentence or lawfully committed to custody, not merely charged -- drawing much heavier punishment at every tier, up to life imprisonment where the escapee was under sentence of death.
essential_elements: accused is a public servant legally bound to apprehend or keep in confinement a person under sentence of a Court, or lawfully committed to custody
intentional omission to apprehend, OR intentionally suffering escape, OR intentionally aiding escape or attempted escape

punishment tier set by the sentence: death sentence (life imprisonment or up to 14 years + fine); life/10+-years sentence (up to 7 years + fine); lesser sentence or lawful committal (up to 3 years, fine, or both)
breakdown.how_to_read: Compare the punishment tiers directly against Section 259: for an equivalent category of underlying offence severity, Section 260 (already-sentenced or lawfully-committed persons) punishes the public servant's complicity roughly twice as severely as Section 259 (merely charged or liable persons) -- the Sanhita treats letting a convicted/committed person escape as markedly graver than letting a charged person escape.

sections.title: Escape from confinement or custody negligently suffered by public servant
sections.raw_text: Whoever, being a public servant legally bound as such public servant to keep in confinement any person charged with or convicted of any offence or lawfully committed to custody, negligently suffers such person to escape from confinement, shall be punished with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.
key_terms: negligently suffering an escape from confinement

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 261 BNS is the negligence-based residual offence alongside Sections 259-260's intentional omission offences -- where a public servant merely negligently (not intentionally) lets a confined person escape, the punishment is capped at two years' simple imprisonment regardless of the escapee's status or underlying offence severity.
essential_elements: accused is a public servant legally bound to keep in confinement a person charged with, convicted of, or lawfully committed in custody for, an offence
negligently (as opposed to intentionally) suffering that person to escape from confinement
breakdown.how_to_read: The mental-state threshold is the whole story here: swap 'intentionally' for 'negligently' and the graduated, offence-severity-linked tiers of Sections 259-260 collapse into one flat, much lighter punishment band -- negligence is treated far more leniently than deliberate complicity in escape.

sections.title: Resistance or obstruction by a person to his lawful apprehension
sections.raw_text:
Whoever intentionally offers any resistance or illegal obstruction to the lawful apprehension of himself for any offence with which he is charged or of which he has been convicted, or escapes or attempts to escape from any custody in which he is lawfully detained for any such offence, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.

Explanation.--The punishment in this section is in addition to the punishment for which the person charged with or convicted of the offence for which he was in custody, would be liable on conviction for such offence.
key_terms: resisting or obstructing one's own lawful apprehension
escaping or attempting escape from lawful custody

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 262 BNS criminalises the flip side of Sections 259-261 -- not the public servant's failure to apprehend, but the apprehended person's own deliberate resistance, illegal obstruction, or escape attempt, punishable up to two years, explicitly stacked on top of punishment for the underlying offence.
essential_elements: intentional resistance or illegal obstruction to one's own lawful apprehension for a charged or convicted offence, OR escaping or attempting to escape from lawful custody for such an offence
exceptions_and_qualifications: The Explanation confirms this punishment is in addition to, not instead of, the punishment for the underlying offence for which the person was in custody.
breakdown.how_to_read: The 'in addition to' Explanation is the key operative point -- a person who both commits an offence and then resists lawful apprehension for it faces cumulative, not concurrent-by-default, criminal exposure; always check whether a resistance/escape charge is being added onto the underlying charge rather than substituted for it.

sections.title: Resistance or obstruction to lawful apprehension of another person
key_terms: resisting or obstructing the lawful apprehension of another person
rescuing or attempting to rescue another person from lawful custody

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 263 BNS is the third-party mirror of Section 262 -- resisting or obstructing someone else's lawful apprehension, or rescuing them from lawful custody, with five escalating punishment tiers driven by the severity of the offence the apprehended/rescued person faces or the sentence they are already serving.
essential_elements: intentional resistance or illegal obstruction to the lawful apprehension of another person for an offence, OR rescuing/attempting to rescue another person from lawful custody for an offence
base punishment up to two years (tier (a))
escalating tiers (b)-(e) keyed to the apprehended/rescued person's offence severity or existing sentence, up to life imprisonment or ten years where that person was under sentence of death
breakdown.how_to_read: The five tiers mirror the same severity ladder used in Sections 259-260 for the public servant's own complicity, but applied here to a private third party who interferes with someone else's lawful apprehension or custody -- always check which of the five sub-clauses the facts fall under before assuming the lightest band applies.

sections.title: Omission to apprehend, or sufferance of escape, on part of public servant, in cases not otherwise provided for
sections.raw_text:
Whoever, being a public servant legally bound as such public servant to apprehend or to keep in confinement any person in any case not provided for in section 259, section 260 or section 261, omits to apprehend that person or suffers him to escape from confinement, shall be punished--

(a) if he does so intentionally, with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both; and

(b) if he does so negligently, with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.
key_terms: residual omission to apprehend or sufferance of escape

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 264 BNS is the catch-all residual provision for public-servant apprehension/confinement duties not already covered by Sections 259-261 -- splitting, like those sections, into an intentional band (up to three years) and a negligent band (up to two years, simple imprisonment).
essential_elements: accused is a public servant legally bound to apprehend or keep in confinement a person, in a case not already covered by Sections 259, 260, or 261
omission to apprehend, or suffering the person to escape from confinement
intentional conduct draws up to three years (any imprisonment description); negligent conduct draws up to two years simple imprisonment
breakdown.how_to_read: Treat this as the fallback bucket: only reach for Section 264 once you've confirmed the facts don't fit neatly into Sections 259 (charged/liable persons), 260 (sentenced/committed persons), or 261 (negligent escape from confinement) -- it exists precisely to avoid a gap in coverage.

sections.title: Resistance or obstruction to lawful apprehension, or escape or rescue, in cases not otherwise provided for
sections.raw_text: Whoever, in any case not provided for in section 262 or section 263, intentionally offers any resistance or illegal obstruction to the lawful apprehension of himself or any other person, or escapes or attempts to escape from any custody in which he is lawfully detained, or rescues or attempts to rescue any person from any custody in which that person is lawfully detained, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine, or with both.
key_terms: residual resistance obstruction escape or rescue

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 265 BNS is the catch-all residual counterpart to Section 264, mirroring its relationship to Sections 262-263 -- a single flat punishment band of up to six months for resistance, obstruction, escape, or rescue not already covered by those two targeted sections.
essential_elements: a case not already covered by Sections 262 or 263

intentional resistance or illegal obstruction to one's own or another's lawful apprehension, OR escaping/attempting to escape from lawful custody, OR rescuing/attempting to rescue another from lawful custody
breakdown.how_to_read: Note the much lighter residual punishment here (up to six months) compared to the specifically targeted Sections 262 (up to two years) and 263 (up to seven years at the top tier) -- residual, catch-all coverage is deliberately punished more lightly than the enumerated, severity-graded scenarios.

sections.title: Violation of condition of remission of punishment
sections.raw_text: Whoever, having accepted any conditional remission of punishment, knowingly violates any condition on which such remission was granted, shall be punished with the punishment to which he was originally sentenced, if he has already suffered no part of that punishment, and if he has suffered any part of that punishment, then with so much of that punishment as he has not already suffered.
key_terms: knowing violation of a condition of remission

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 266 BNS enforces the conditional nature of a remission of sentence -- a person who accepts conditional remission and then knowingly breaks a condition of it is put back on the hook for the original sentence, minus whatever portion they have already served.
essential_elements: accused had accepted a conditional remission of punishment
knowing violation of a condition attached to that remission
breakdown.how_to_read: The remedy is restorative, not additive -- the violator doesn't get a fresh, separate punishment on top of everything else; they simply forfeit the benefit of remission and must serve the unserved remainder (or the whole original sentence if none was yet served).

sections.title: Intentional insult or interruption to public servant sitting in judicial proceeding
sections.raw_text: Whoever intentionally offers any insult, or causes any interruption to any public servant, while such public servant is sitting in any stage of a judicial proceeding, shall be punished with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine which may extend to five thousand rupees, or with both.
key_terms: intentional insult or interruption to a public servant in a judicial proceeding

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 267 BNS is the Sanhita's contempt-of-court-adjacent offence -- intentionally insulting or interrupting a public servant while they are sitting in any stage of a judicial proceeding, punishable with up to six months' simple imprisonment, fine up to five thousand rupees, or both.
essential_elements: intentional insult, or causing interruption, to a public servant
the public servant is sitting in any stage of a judicial proceeding at the time
breakdown.how_to_read: 'Any stage of a judicial proceeding' carries the same broad meaning developed under Section 229's Explanations (including Court-directed preliminary investigations and courts-martial) -- this isn't limited to disrupting a trial judge mid-hearing in a conventional courtroom.

sections.title: Personation of assessor
sections.raw_text: Whoever, by personation or otherwise, intentionally causes or suffers himself to be returned, empanelled or sworn as an assessor in any case in which he knows that he is not entitled by law to be so returned, empanelled or sworn, or knowing himself to have been so returned, empanelled or sworn contrary to law, voluntarily serves on such case as an assessor, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.
key_terms: personation of an assessor
knowingly serving as an assessor when not legally entitled

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 268 BNS targets fraudulent or otherwise unlawful participation as a court assessor -- either by personation/other means causing oneself to be returned, empanelled, or sworn as an assessor when not legally entitled, or by knowingly and voluntarily serving despite knowing the selection was unlawful.
essential_elements: by personation or otherwise, intentionally causing or suffering oneself to be returned, empanelled, or sworn as an assessor while knowing one is not legally entitled, OR
knowing oneself to have been returned, empanelled, or sworn as an assessor contrary to law, and voluntarily serving on the case regardless
breakdown.how_to_read: The two limbs cover both ends of the timeline: fraudulently engineering one's own unlawful selection in the first place, and separately, discovering after the fact that one's selection was unlawful yet choosing to serve anyway -- either suffices independently.

sections.title: Failure by person released on bail bond or bond to appear in Court
sections.raw_text:
Whoever, being released on bail bond or bond, fails without sufficient cause (which shall be proved by him) to appear in Court in accordance with the terms of the bail bond or bond, shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to one year, or with fine, or with both.

Explanation.--The punishment under this section is--

(a) in addition to the punishment to which such person would be otherwise liable on conviction for the offence with which he has been charged or convicted; and

(b) without prejudice to the power of the Court to order forfeiture of the bond under section 491 of the Bhartiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023.
key_terms: failure to appear in court per bail bond or bond terms
burden of proof on the accused to show sufficient cause for non-appearance

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 269 BNS, closing Chapter XIV, is the Sanhita's bail-jumping offence -- a person released on bail bond or bond who fails, without sufficient cause, to appear in Court per the bond's terms is separately punishable with up to one year's imprisonment, fine, or both, on top of consequences for the underlying charged offence and independent of the Court's own bond-forfeiture power.
essential_elements: accused was released on a bail bond or bond
failure to appear in Court in accordance with that bond's terms
absence of sufficient cause for the non-appearance, with the burden of proving sufficient cause resting on the accused
exceptions_and_qualifications: Punishment under this section is in addition to whatever the accused is otherwise liable to on conviction for the underlying charged offence (Explanation (a)).
This punishment operates without prejudice to the Court's separate power to order forfeiture of the bond under BNSS Section 491 (Explanation (b)).
breakdown.how_to_read: Note the reversed burden of proof -- unlike most BNS offences where the prosecution bears the burden throughout, here the accused must affirmatively prove sufficient cause for non-appearance once the bare fact of non-appearance is shown; and like Section 262, this punishment stacks rather than substitutes.

sections.title: Public nuisance
sections.raw_text: A person is guilty of a public nuisance who does any act or is guilty of an illegal omission which causes any common injury, danger or annoyance to the public or to the people in general who dwell or occupy property in the vicinity, or which must necessarily cause injury, obstruction, danger or annoyance to persons who may have occasion to use any public right but a common nuisance is not excused on the ground that it causes some convenience or advantage.
key_terms: public nuisance
common injury danger or annoyance to the public

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 270 BNS opens Chapter XV by defining 'public nuisance' -- any act or illegal omission causing common injury, danger, or annoyance to the public or to people dwelling/occupying property nearby, or that necessarily obstructs or endangers anyone exercising a public right. This definition anchors every specific offence in the rest of the chapter.
essential_elements: an act, or an illegal omission

causing common injury, danger, or annoyance to the public, or to people who dwell/occupy property in the vicinity, OR necessarily causing injury, obstruction, danger, or annoyance to persons exercising a public right
exceptions_and_qualifications: A common nuisance is not excused merely because it also causes some convenience or advantage.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is a pure definition section, not a standalone punishment provision -- Section 292 supplies the residual punishment for public nuisance 'in cases not otherwise punishable by this Sanhita,' while specific nuisances throughout the chapter (noxious food, polluted water, rash driving, etc.) carry their own tailored punishments.

sections.title: Negligent act likely to spread infection of disease dangerous to life
sections.raw_text: Whoever unlawfully or negligently does any act which is, and which he knows or has reason to believe to be, likely to spread the infection of any disease dangerous to life, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine, or with both.
key_terms: negligent act likely to spread infection of a life-dangerous disease

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 271 BNS criminalises unlawfully or negligently doing an act one knows or has reason to believe is likely to spread a life-dangerous disease's infection -- the lighter, negligence-based counterpart to Section 272's malignant-intent version of the same conduct.
essential_elements: an act done unlawfully or negligently
the act is, and the accused knows or has reason to believe it to be, likely to spread the infection of a disease dangerous to life
breakdown.how_to_read: Pair this with Section 272 -- the conduct described (spreading infection of a life-dangerous disease) is identical, but Section 271's maximum (six months) is a quarter of Section 272's maximum (two years) because the mental state here is negligence/unlawfulness rather than malignancy.

sections.title: Malignant act likely to spread infection of disease dangerous to life
sections.raw_text: Whoever malignantly does any act which is, and which he knows or has reason to believe to be, likely to spread the infection of any disease dangerous to life, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.
key_terms: malignant act likely to spread infection of a life-dangerous disease

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 272 BNS is the aggravated, malignant-intent counterpart to Section 271 -- doing an act malignantly (rather than merely negligently) that one knows or has reason to believe is likely to spread a life-dangerous disease's infection, punishable up to two years.
essential_elements: an act done malignantly
the act is, and the accused knows or has reason to believe it to be, likely to spread the infection of a disease dangerous to life
breakdown.how_to_read: 'Malignantly' signals a deliberately harmful state of mind distinct from the negligence/unlawfulness standard in Section 271 -- the four-fold jump in maximum sentence (six months to two years) tracks this sharper mental-state distinction.

sections.title: Disobedience to quarantine rule
sections.raw_text: Whoever knowingly disobeys any rule made by the Government for putting any mode of transport into a state of quarantine, or for regulating the intercourse of any such transport in a state of quarantine or for regulating the intercourse between places where an infectious disease prevails and other places, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine, or with both.
key_terms: knowing disobedience to a quarantine rule

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 273 BNS criminalises knowingly disobeying a Government-made quarantine rule -- whether the rule puts transport into quarantine, regulates quarantined transport's intercourse, or regulates movement between infected and uninfected places -- punishable with up to six months' imprisonment, fine, or both.
essential_elements: a rule made by the Government relating to quarantine of transport, or intercourse regulation involving quarantined transport or infectious-disease-affected places
knowing disobedience of that rule
breakdown.how_to_read: This is a public-health regulatory-compliance offence, complementing Sections 271-272's substantive disease-spreading offences by criminalising the breach of the administrative mechanism (quarantine rules) designed to prevent spread in the first place.

sections.title: Adulteration of food or drink intended for sale
sections.raw_text: Whoever adulterates any article of food or drink, so as to make such article noxious as food or drink, intending to sell such article as food or drink, or knowing it to be likely that the same will be sold as food or drink, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine which may extend to five thousand rupees, or with both.
key_terms: adulterating food or drink to make it noxious for intended sale

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 274 BNS opens the food/drug-safety cluster of Chapter XV -- adulterating a food or drink article so as to make it noxious, while intending it to be sold as food/drink or knowing it is likely to be sold as such, punishable with up to six months plus fine up to five thousand rupees.
essential_elements: adulterating an article of food or drink so as to make it noxious as food or drink
intention to sell the article as food or drink, OR knowledge that it is likely to be so sold
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the adulteration (manufacturing/tampering) offence; Section 275 is its selling-side mirror for already-noxious food or drink -- together they cover both the creation and the distribution ends of the unsafe-food-supply chain.

sections.title: Sale of noxious food or drink
sections.raw_text: Whoever sells, or offers or exposes for sale, as food or drink, any article which has been rendered or has become noxious, or is in a state unfit for food or drink, knowing or having reason to believe that the same is noxious as food or drink, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine which may extend to five thousand rupees, or with both.
key_terms: selling food or drink known to be noxious or unfit

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 275 BNS is the selling-side mirror of Section 274 -- selling, offering, or exposing for sale as food/drink any article rendered noxious or unfit, while knowing or having reason to believe it is noxious, punished identically to adulteration.
essential_elements: selling, offering, or exposing for sale as food or drink an article that has been rendered or has become noxious, or is unfit for food or drink
knowledge or reason to believe that the article is noxious as food or drink
breakdown.how_to_read: Notice this offence doesn't require the seller to have done the adulterating themselves -- merely knowingly selling already-noxious food or drink, regardless of who made it noxious, completes the offence.

sections.title: Adulteration of drugs
sections.raw_text: Whoever adulterates any drug or medical preparation in such a manner as to lessen the efficacy or change the operation of such drug or medical preparation, or to make it noxious, intending that it shall be sold or used for, or knowing it to be likely that it will be sold or used for, any medicinal purpose, as if it had not undergone such adulteration, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to one year, or with fine which may extend to five thousand rupees, or with both.
key_terms: adulterating a drug or medical preparation to lessen efficacy or make it noxious

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 276 BNS is the drug-safety counterpart to Section 274's food-adulteration offence -- adulterating a drug or medical preparation so as to lessen its efficacy, change its operation, or make it noxious, intending or knowing it likely that it will be sold/used for a medicinal purpose as if unadulterated, punishable with up to one year plus fine up to five thousand rupees.
essential_elements: adulterating a drug or medical preparation in a manner that lessens its efficacy, changes its operation, or makes it noxious
intention that it be sold or used for a medicinal purpose (as if unadulterated), OR knowledge that it is likely to be so sold or used
breakdown.how_to_read: The one-year maximum here is double Section 274's food-adulteration maximum (six months), reflecting the heightened danger of tampering with medicinal products that people rely on for treatment.

sections.title: Sale of adulterated drugs
sections.raw_text: Whoever, knowing any drug or medical preparation to have been adulterated in such a manner as to lessen its efficacy, to change its operation, or to render it noxious, sells the same, or offers or exposes it for sale, or issues it from any dispensary for medicinal purposes as unadulterated, or causes it to be used for medicinal purposes by any person not knowing of the adulteration, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine which may extend to five thousand rupees, or with both.
key_terms: selling or dispensing adulterated drugs as unadulterated

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 277 BNS is the selling/dispensing-side mirror of Section 276 -- knowingly selling, offering for sale, issuing from a dispensary, or causing the use of an adulterated drug for medicinal purposes as if unadulterated, punishable with up to six months plus fine up to five thousand rupees.
essential_elements: knowledge that a drug or medical preparation has been adulterated in a manner lessening its efficacy, changing its operation, or rendering it noxious
selling it, offering/exposing it for sale, issuing it from a dispensary for medicinal purposes as unadulterated, or causing its use for medicinal purposes by someone unaware of the adulteration
breakdown.how_to_read: As with Section 275's relationship to Section 274, this offence targets the distribution/dispensing end of the adulterated-drug chain -- the seller or dispenser need not have done the adulterating themselves, only knowingly pass off the adulterated product as genuine.

sections.title: Sale of drug as a different drug or preparation
sections.raw_text: Whoever knowingly sells, or offers or exposes for sale, or issues from a dispensary for medicinal purposes, any drug or medical preparation, as a different drug or medical preparation, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine which may extend to five thousand rupees, or with both.
key_terms: selling a drug as a different drug or preparation

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 278 BNS covers drug-substitution misrepresentation -- knowingly selling, offering for sale, or dispensing a drug or medical preparation as if it were a different drug or preparation, punishable identically to selling adulterated drugs under Section 277.
essential_elements: knowingly selling, offering/exposing for sale, or issuing from a dispensary for medicinal purposes, a drug or medical preparation
misrepresenting it as a different drug or medical preparation than it actually is
breakdown.how_to_read: This is distinct from adulteration (Sections 276-277) -- the drug need not be tampered with or impure at all; the offence is purely about mislabelling or misrepresenting one genuine drug as being a different one, which is independently dangerous given how medicinal dosing and effects vary by drug.

sections.title: Fouling water of public spring or reservoir
sections.raw_text: Whoever voluntarily corrupts or fouls the water of any public spring or reservoir, so as to render it less fit for the purpose for which it is ordinarily used, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine which may extend to five thousand rupees, or with both.
key_terms: voluntarily fouling water of a public spring or reservoir

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 279 BNS protects public water sources -- voluntarily corrupting or fouling the water of a public spring or reservoir so as to render it less fit for its ordinary use, punishable with up to six months plus fine up to five thousand rupees.
essential_elements: voluntarily corrupting or fouling water of a public spring or reservoir
the corruption/fouling renders the water less fit for the purpose for which it is ordinarily used
breakdown.how_to_read: The harm threshold is relatively low -- the water need only be rendered 'less fit' for its ordinary use, not rendered completely unusable or proven to have caused actual illness, reflecting the preventive, public-health-protective character of this offence.

sections.title: Making atmosphere noxious to health
sections.raw_text: Whoever voluntarily vitiates the atmosphere in any place so as to make it noxious to the health of persons in general dwelling or carrying on business in the neighbourhood or passing along a public way, shall be punished with fine which may extend to one thousand rupees.
key_terms: voluntarily vitiating the atmosphere to make it noxious to health

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 280 BNS is an early air-pollution offence -- voluntarily vitiating the atmosphere in a place so as to make it noxious to the health of people generally dwelling, working, or passing by nearby, punishable only with a fine up to one thousand rupees (no imprisonment option).
essential_elements: voluntarily vitiating the atmosphere in a place
the vitiation makes the atmosphere noxious to the health of persons generally dwelling, carrying on business in the neighbourhood, or passing along a public way
breakdown.how_to_read: Notice this is fine-only, unlike almost every other offence in this cluster -- reflecting its position as the lightest of the environmental/public-health nuisance offences in the chapter, though still capturing genuine atmospheric harm affecting a general neighbourhood population.

sections.title: Rash driving or riding on a public way
sections.raw_text: Whoever drives any vehicle, or rides, on any public way in a manner so rash or negligent as to endanger human life, or to be likely to cause hurt or injury to any other person, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine which may extend to one thousand rupees, or with both.
key_terms: rash or negligent driving or riding on a public way

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 281 BNS is the general rash/negligent driving or riding offence -- operating a vehicle or riding on a public way so rashly or negligently as to endanger human life or be likely to cause hurt or injury, punishable with up to six months plus fine up to one thousand rupees.
essential_elements: driving a vehicle, or riding, on a public way
in a manner so rash or negligent as to endanger human life, or to be likely to cause hurt or injury to another person
breakdown.how_to_read: This sits alongside Section 282's parallel offence for rash navigation of a vessel -- together the two sections cover the land-transport and water-transport analogues of dangerous operation endangering public safety.

sections.title: Rash navigation of vessel
sections.raw_text: Whoever navigates any vessel in a manner so rash or negligent as to endanger human life, or to be likely to cause hurt or injury to any other person, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine which may extend to ten thousand rupees, or with both.
key_terms: rash or negligent navigation of a vessel

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 282 BNS is the water-transport mirror of Section 281's rash-driving offence -- navigating any vessel so rashly or negligently as to endanger human life or be likely to cause hurt or injury, punishable with up to six months plus fine up to ten thousand rupees (a higher fine ceiling than Section 281's land-based equivalent).
essential_elements: navigating any vessel
in a manner so rash or negligent as to endanger human life, or to be likely to cause hurt or injury to another person
breakdown.how_to_read: The fine ceiling here (ten thousand rupees) is ten times Section 281's (one thousand rupees) despite an identical imprisonment ceiling -- reflecting the generally higher stakes and scale of harm typically associated with reckless vessel navigation.

sections.title: Exhibition of false light, mark or buoy
sections.raw_text: Whoever exhibits any false light, mark or buoy, intending or knowing it to be likely that such exhibition will mislead any navigator, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and with fine which shall not be less than ten thousand rupees.
key_terms: exhibiting a false light mark or buoy to mislead navigators

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 283 BNS sharply escalates punishment within the maritime-safety cluster -- exhibiting a false light, mark, or buoy, intending or knowing it likely to mislead a navigator, is punishable with up to seven years' imprisonment plus a mandatory minimum fine of ten thousand rupees, by far the heaviest offence in this part of the chapter.
essential_elements: exhibiting a false light, mark, or buoy
intention, or knowledge of likelihood, that the exhibition will mislead a navigator
breakdown.how_to_read: The mandatory minimum fine (not less than ten thousand rupees, with no stated upper cap) is unusual within this chapter's otherwise fine-capped offences, and the seven-year maximum imprisonment reflects the potentially catastrophic consequences of deliberately misleading maritime navigation -- shipwrecks, mass casualties -- that this conduct risks.

sections.title: Conveying person by water for hire in unsafe or overloaded vessel
sections.raw_text: Whoever knowingly or negligently conveys, or causes to be conveyed for hire, any person by water in any vessel, when that vessel is in such a state or so loaded as to endanger the life of that person, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine which may extend to five thousand rupees, or with both.
key_terms: conveying a person for hire in an unsafe or overloaded vessel

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 284 BNS protects paying passengers on water transport -- knowingly or negligently conveying, or causing to be conveyed, a person for hire by water in a vessel so unsafe or overloaded as to endanger that person's life, punishable with up to six months plus fine up to five thousand rupees.
essential_elements: conveying, or causing to be conveyed, a person by water in a vessel, for hire
the vessel's state or loading endangers the life of that person
knowledge or negligence as to the unsafe state or overloading
breakdown.how_to_read: This sits alongside Section 282's rash-navigation offence but targets a distinct wrong -- not reckless operation of an otherwise sound vessel, but putting a paying passenger on a vessel that is inherently unsafe or overloaded in the first place.

sections.title: Danger or obstruction in public way or line of navigation
sections.raw_text: Whoever, by doing any act, or by omitting to take order with any property in his possession or under his charge, causes danger, obstruction or injury to any person in any public way or public line of navigation, shall be punished with fine which may extend to five thousand rupees.
key_terms: causing danger obstruction or injury in a public way or line of navigation

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 285 BNS is a fine-only offence covering both acts and omissions -- doing any act, or omitting to properly manage property in one's possession or charge, so as to cause danger, obstruction, or injury to anyone in a public way or public line of navigation, punishable with fine up to five thousand rupees.
essential_elements: an act, or an omission to take order with property in one's possession or under one's charge
causing danger, obstruction, or injury to a person in a public way or public line of navigation
breakdown.how_to_read: Like Section 280, this is fine-only with no imprisonment option -- it functions as a broad catch-all for public-way/navigation-line obstruction that doesn't rise to the level of the more specific, imprisonment-carrying negligence offences in Sections 286-291.

sections.title: Negligent conduct with respect to poisonous substance
sections.raw_text: Whoever does, with any poisonous substance, any act in a manner so rash or negligent as to endanger human life, or to be likely to cause hurt or injury to any person or knowingly or negligently omits to take such order with any poisonous substance in his possession as is sufficient to guard against any probable danger to human life from such poisonous substance, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine which may extend to five thousand rupees, or with both.
key_terms: rash or negligent act with a poisonous substance
negligent omission to safeguard a poisonous substance

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 286 BNS opens a cluster of near-identically structured negligence offences tied to specific categories of inherently dangerous things -- here, poisonous substances. Either rashly/negligently acting with a poisonous substance so as to endanger life, or knowingly/negligently failing to take sufficient safeguarding precautions with one in one's possession, draws up to six months plus fine up to five thousand rupees.
essential_elements: doing an act with a poisonous substance in a manner so rash or negligent as to endanger human life or be likely to cause hurt or injury, OR
knowingly or negligently omitting to take sufficient precautions with a poisonous substance in one's possession to guard against probable danger to human life
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the first of six structurally parallel 'negligent conduct with respect to X' offences (Sections 286-291, covering poisonous substances, fire/combustible matter, explosives, machinery, buildings, and animals) -- each pairs an active-rash-act limb with a passive-failure-to-safeguard limb, both carrying identical punishment ranges except where noted.

sections.title: Negligent conduct with respect to fire or combustible matter
sections.raw_text: Whoever does, with fire or any combustible matter, any act so rashly or negligently as to endanger human life, or to be likely to cause hurt or injury to any other person or knowingly or negligently omits to take such order with any fire or any combustible matter in his possession as is sufficient to guard against any probable danger to human life from such fire or combustible matter, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine which may extend to two thousand rupees, or with both.
key_terms: rash or negligent act with fire or combustible matter
negligent omission to safeguard fire or combustible matter

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 287 BNS applies the same rash-act/failure-to-safeguard structure as Section 286, but to fire or combustible matter -- punishable with up to six months plus fine up to two thousand rupees (a lower fine ceiling than the poisonous-substance offence).
essential_elements: doing an act with fire or combustible matter in a manner so rash or negligent as to endanger human life or be likely to cause hurt or injury, OR
knowingly or negligently omitting to take sufficient precautions with fire or combustible matter in one's possession to guard against probable danger to human life
breakdown.how_to_read: Compare the fine ceilings across this cluster of sections -- they are not uniform (five thousand for poison, two thousand for fire, five thousand for explosives and machinery and buildings) even though imprisonment ceilings are identical at six months throughout.

sections.title: Negligent conduct with respect to explosive substance
sections.raw_text: Whoever does, with any explosive substance, any act so rashly or negligently as to endanger human life, or to be likely to cause hurt or injury to any other person, or knowingly or negligently omits to take such order with any explosive substance in his possession as is sufficient to guard against any probable danger to human life from that substance, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine which may extend to five thousand rupees, or with both.
key_terms: rash or negligent act with an explosive substance
negligent omission to safeguard an explosive substance

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 288 BNS continues the structural pattern for explosive substances -- rashly/negligently acting with an explosive so as to endanger life, or failing to safeguard one sufficiently, punishable with up to six months plus fine up to five thousand rupees.
essential_elements: doing an act with an explosive substance in a manner so rash or negligent as to endanger human life or be likely to cause hurt or injury, OR
knowingly or negligently omitting to take sufficient precautions with an explosive substance in one's possession to guard against probable danger to human life
breakdown.how_to_read: Note this section's relatively modest six-month maximum applies only to the negligence-based conduct covered here -- deliberate, intentional misuse of explosives to cause harm falls instead under the much heavier body-offence or property-offence provisions elsewhere in the Sanhita, not this section.

sections.title: Negligent conduct with respect to machinery
sections.raw_text: Whoever does, with any machinery, any act so rashly or negligently as to endanger human life or to be likely to cause hurt or injury to any other person or knowingly or negligently omits to take such order with any machinery in his possession or under his care as is sufficient to guard against any probable danger to human life from such machinery, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine which may extend to five thousand rupees, or with both.
key_terms: rash or negligent act with machinery
negligent omission to safeguard machinery

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 289 BNS applies the same structure to machinery -- rashly/negligently operating machinery so as to endanger life, or failing to sufficiently safeguard machinery in one's possession or care, punishable with up to six months plus fine up to five thousand rupees.
essential_elements: doing an act with machinery in a manner so rash or negligent as to endanger human life or be likely to cause hurt or injury, OR
knowingly or negligently omitting to take sufficient precautions with machinery in one's possession or under one's care to guard against probable danger to human life
breakdown.how_to_read: The phrase 'in his possession or under his care' (slightly broader than the 'in his possession' wording used for poison, fire, and explosives) extends this offence to machinery one merely has custodial responsibility for, even without strict legal possession.

sections.title: Negligent conduct with respect to pulling down, repairing or constructing buildings, etc.
sections.raw_text: Whoever, in pulling down, repairing or constructing any building, knowingly or negligently omits to take such measures with that building as is sufficient to guard against any probable danger to human life from the fall of that building, or of any part thereof, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine which may extend to five thousand rupees, or with both.
key_terms: negligent omission to safeguard against building collapse during demolition repair or construction

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 290 BNS targets construction-site safety -- a person pulling down, repairing, or constructing a building who knowingly or negligently omits sufficient safety measures against the probable danger of the building (or part of it) falling, punishable with up to six months plus fine up to five thousand rupees.
essential_elements: pulling down, repairing, or constructing a building
knowing or negligent omission to take measures sufficient to guard against probable danger to human life from the fall of that building or any part of it
breakdown.how_to_read: Unlike Sections 286-289, this section has only a single omission-based limb (no separate 'rash act' limb) -- the offence is specifically about failing to safeguard during demolition, repair, or construction work, not about rashly operating equipment in the process.

sections.title: Negligent conduct with respect to animal
sections.raw_text: Whoever knowingly or negligently omits to take such measures with any animal in his possession as is sufficient to guard against any probable danger to human life, or any probable danger of grievous hurt from such animal, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine which may extend to five thousand rupees, or with both.
key_terms: negligent omission to safeguard against danger from an animal

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 291 BNS closes the negligence-offence cluster -- knowingly or negligently omitting sufficient safeguarding measures with an animal in one's possession, guarding against probable danger to human life or probable grievous hurt, punishable with up to six months plus fine up to five thousand rupees.
essential_elements: possession of an animal
knowing or negligent omission to take measures sufficient to guard against probable danger to human life, or probable danger of grievous hurt, from that animal
breakdown.how_to_read: Like Section 290, this is a single omission-based limb -- the offence targets failure to safeguard against a dangerous animal one possesses, not any rash act done 'with' the animal; this closes out the six-section negligence cluster (286-291) before the chapter returns to nuisance and obscenity offences.

sections.title: Punishment for public nuisance in cases not otherwise provided for
sections.raw_text: Whoever commits a public nuisance in any case not otherwise punishable by this Sanhita shall be punished with fine which may extend to one thousand rupees.
key_terms: residual punishment for public nuisance

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 292 BNS supplies the residual, catch-all punishment for the Section 270 public-nuisance definition -- where conduct fits the definition of public nuisance but isn't already specifically punished elsewhere in the Sanhita (e.g. by Sections 271-291's targeted offences), this fine-only provision (up to one thousand rupees) applies.
essential_elements: conduct that constitutes a public nuisance within the Section 270 definition
the conduct is not otherwise punishable under any other provision of the Sanhita
breakdown.how_to_read: Always check the more specific provisions first (Sections 271-291, and others scattered through the Sanhita) before falling back on Section 292 -- it exists precisely to avoid a gap in coverage for public-nuisance conduct that doesn't fit any more targeted offence.

sections.title: Continuance of nuisance after injunction to discontinue
sections.raw_text: Whoever repeats or continues a public nuisance, having been enjoined by any public servant who has lawful authority to issue such injunction not to repeat or continue such nuisance, shall be punished with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine which may extend to five thousand rupees, or with both.
key_terms: repeating or continuing a nuisance after a lawful injunction to discontinue

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 293 BNS escalates liability where a public nuisance continues despite an official order to stop -- repeating or continuing a public nuisance after being enjoined by a public servant with lawful authority to issue such an injunction, punishable with up to six months' simple imprisonment plus fine up to five thousand rupees, far heavier than Section 292's plain fine-only residual punishment.
essential_elements: repeating or continuing a public nuisance
having been enjoined (ordered to stop) by a public servant with lawful authority to issue such an injunction
breakdown.how_to_read: The jump from Section 292's fine-only residual punishment to this section's imprisonment-carrying punishment illustrates a recurring theme in the Sanhita -- defiance of a specific lawful official order is treated as substantially more serious than the underlying primary conduct alone.

sections.title: Sale, etc., of obscene books, etc.
sections.raw_text:
(1) For the purposes of sub-section (2), a book, pamphlet, paper, writing, drawing, painting, representation, figure or any other object, including display of any content in electronic form shall be deemed to be obscene if it is lascivious or appeals to the prurient interest or if its effect, or (where it comprises two or more distinct items) the effect of any one of its items, is, if taken as a whole, such as to tend to deprave and corrupt persons who are likely, having regard to all relevant circumstances, to read, see or hear the matter contained or embodied in it.

(2) Whoever--

(a) sells, lets to hire, distributes, publicly exhibits or in any manner puts into circulation, or for purposes of sale, hire, distribution, public exhibition or circulation, makes, produces or has in his possession any obscene book, pamphlet, paper, drawing, painting, representation or figure or any other obscene object whatsoever in whatever manner; or

(b) imports, exports or conveys any obscene object for any of the purposes aforesaid, or knowing or having reason to believe that such object will be sold, let to hire, distributed or publicly exhibited or in any manner put into circulation; or

(c) takes part in or receives profits from any business in the course of which he knows or has reason to believe that any such obscene objects are, for any of the purposes aforesaid, made produced, purchased, kept, imported, exported, conveyed, publicly exhibited or in any manner put into circulation; or

(d) advertises or makes known by any means whatsoever that any person is engaged or is ready to engage in any act which is an offence under this section, or that any such obscene object can be procured from or through any person; or

(e) offers or attempts to do any act which is an offence under this section,

shall be punished on first conviction with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, and with fine which may extend to five thousand rupees, and, in the event of a second or subsequent conviction, with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to five years, and also with fine which may extend to ten thousand rupees.

Exception.--This section does not extend to--

(a) any book, pamphlet, paper, writing, drawing, painting, representation or figure--

(i) the publication of which is proved to be justified as being for the public good on the ground that such book, pamphlet, paper, writing, drawing, painting, representation or figure is in the interest of science, literature, art or learning or other objects of general concern; or

(ii) which is kept or used bona fide for religious purposes;

(b) any representation sculptured, engraved, painted or otherwise represented on or in--

(i) any ancient monument within the meaning of the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, 1958; or

(ii) any temple, or on any car used for the conveyance of idols, or kept or used for any religious purpose.
key_terms: obscenity test for books and other objects including electronic content
selling distributing or circulating obscene objects
public-good and bona fide religious-use exceptions to obscenity

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 294 BNS defines what counts as 'obscene' (lascivious, appealing to prurient interest, or tending to deprave and corrupt likely readers/viewers/listeners, taking the work as a whole, and expressly extending to electronic-form content) and then criminalises a broad range of conduct around obscene material -- selling, hiring, distributing, exhibiting, producing, importing/exporting, profiting from, advertising, or attempting any of these -- with escalating punishment for repeat convictions, subject to public-good and bona fide religious-use exceptions.
essential_elements: the material qualifies as 'obscene' under sub-section (1)'s test (lascivious, prurient appeal, or tending to deprave/corrupt likely readers/viewers/listeners taken as a whole)

one of the acts in sub-section (2)(a)-(e) -- selling/hiring/distributing/exhibiting/circulating/producing/possessing for those purposes, importing/exporting/conveying, profiting from such a business, advertising such material or services, or attempting any of the above
first conviction: up to two years plus fine up to five thousand rupees; second or subsequent conviction: up to five years plus fine up to ten thousand rupees
exceptions_and_qualifications: Does not extend to material whose publication is proved justified as being for the public good on grounds of science, literature, art, learning, or other objects of general concern, or kept/used bona fide for religious purposes.

Does not extend to representations on ancient monuments (under the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, 1958) or on temples/idol-conveyance cars kept or used for religious purposes.
breakdown.how_to_read: The sub-section (1) obscenity test ('taken as a whole,' likely-audience-focused) is the threshold question that must be answered before any of the sub-section (2) conduct limbs can apply; always check the Exception next -- genuine scientific, literary, artistic, or bona fide religious material is carved out even if it might otherwise satisfy the obscenity test.

sections.title: Sale, etc., of obscene objects to child
sections.raw_text: Whoever sells, lets to hire, distributes, exhibits or circulates to any child any such obscene object as is referred to in section 294, or offers or attempts so to do, shall be punished on first conviction with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, and with fine which may extend to two thousand rupees, and, in the event of a second or subsequent conviction, with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and also with fine which may extend to five thousand rupees.
key_terms: selling or distributing an obscene object to a child

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 295 BNS is the child-protection escalation of Section 294 -- selling, hiring, distributing, exhibiting, or circulating (or attempting to do any of these with) an obscene object as defined in Section 294, specifically to a child, carrying heavier punishment than the general obscenity offence: up to three years on first conviction, up to seven years on repeat conviction.
essential_elements: an object that qualifies as obscene under Section 294's definition
selling, letting to hire, distributing, exhibiting, or circulating that object to a child, or offering/attempting to do so
first conviction: up to three years plus fine up to two thousand rupees; second or subsequent conviction: up to seven years plus fine up to five thousand rupees
breakdown.how_to_read: Compare directly against Section 294: the imprisonment maximum here is higher at every tier (3 years vs. 2 years on first conviction; 7 years vs. 5 years on repeat) despite a lower first-conviction fine ceiling, reflecting the heightened seriousness the Sanhita attaches to exposing children specifically to obscene material.

sections.title: Obscene acts and songs
sections.raw_text:
Whoever, to the annoyance of others,--

(a) does any obscene act in any public place; or

(b) sings, recites or utters any obscene song, ballad or words, in or near any public place,

shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three months, or with fine which may extend to one thousand rupees, or with both.
key_terms: obscene act in a public place
obscene song ballad or words in or near a public place

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 296 BNS targets live obscene conduct in public, as distinct from Section 294's obscene-material offences -- doing an obscene act in a public place, or singing/reciting/uttering obscene songs, ballads, or words in or near a public place, to the annoyance of others, punishable with up to three months plus fine up to one thousand rupees.
essential_elements: an obscene act in a public place, OR obscene song/ballad/words sung, recited, or uttered in or near a public place
the conduct is to the annoyance of others
breakdown.how_to_read: The 'to the annoyance of others' requirement is an operative element, not mere surplus language -- the prosecution must show the conduct actually annoyed someone, tying this offence conceptually back to the public-nuisance framework opening the chapter even though it sits in the obscenity cluster.

sections.title: Keeping lottery office
sections.raw_text:
(1) Whoever keeps any office or place for the purpose of drawing any lottery not being a State lottery or a lottery authorised by the State Government, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine, or with both.

(2) Whoever publishes any proposal to pay any sum, or to deliver any goods, or to do or forbear from doing anything for the benefit of any person, on any event or contingency relative or applicable to the drawing of any ticket, lot, number or figure in any such lottery, shall be punished with fine which may extend to five thousand rupees.
key_terms: keeping an office for an unauthorised lottery
publishing a proposal tied to the drawing of an unauthorised lottery

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 297 BNS, closing Chapter XV, targets unauthorised lotteries -- keeping an office or place for drawing any lottery that is not a State lottery or a State-Government-authorised lottery (sub-section (1)), and separately, publishing any proposal to pay money, deliver goods, or do/forbear from doing anything contingent on such an unauthorised lottery's drawing (sub-section (2)).
essential_elements: sub-section (1): keeping an office or place for the purpose of drawing a lottery that is neither a State lottery nor one authorised by the State Government

sub-section (2): publishing a proposal to pay a sum, deliver goods, or do/forbear from doing anything for a person's benefit, contingent on the drawing of a ticket, lot, number, or figure in such an unauthorised lottery
exceptions_and_qualifications: State lotteries and lotteries authorised by the State Government fall outside sub-section (1)'s prohibition entirely.
breakdown.how_to_read: The two sub-sections target different points in the unauthorised-lottery chain -- sub-section (1) the operator who keeps the drawing office (imprisonment-eligible), sub-section (2) anyone who publishes lottery-contingent proposals, such as promoters or advertisers (fine-only) -- and both carve out State-run or State-authorised lotteries from the outset.

sections.title: Injuring or defiling place of worship with intent to insult religion of any class
sections.raw_text: Whoever destroys, damages or defiles any place of worship, or any object held sacred by any class of persons with the intention of thereby insulting the religion of any class of persons or with the knowledge that any class of persons is likely to consider such destruction, damage or defilement as an insult to their religion, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.
